questions.text: Define death. Mention the manner of death.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Death:**
In most countries of the world including Bangladesh, there is no clear-cut definition about death in law:
* **Clinically:** Death is defined as "Complete and irreversible cessation of life".
* **Medico-legal definition of death:** Death is permanent and irreversible cessation of functions of the three interlinked vital system of the body (the tripod of life) namely the nervous system, respiratory system and circulatory system.
* **Dictionary definitions:**
  * *Black's Law Dictionary:* "The cessation of life; the ceasing to exist".
  * *Chamber's twentieth century dictionary:* "Extinction of life".
  * *Oxford dictionary:* "The end of life".

**Manner of Death:**
* **Definition:** Manner of death indicates the circumstances under which the person died. Or, Manner of death indicates the design how cause of death has come into action.
* **Types of manners of death:**
  * **A. Natural:** If death occurs exclusively from disease.
  * **B. Unnatural/violent:** If death occurs exclusively from injury or is hastened due to injury in a person suffering from natural disease. Violence may be:
    * Suicidal
    * Homicidal
    * Accidental
    * Undetermined or unexplained

**Guide Book Page:** Page 138 & Page 148

questions.text: Define abrasion. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Abrasion:**
* **Abrasion:** Abrasion is damage or destruction of superficial epithelial covering of skin (epidermis) or mucus membrane, due to impact (mostly frictions) with hard, blunt and rough object or weapon.
* *Or,* Abrasion is temporary loss of superficial epithelial covering of skin (epidermis) or mucus membrane, due to forcible friction of body surface against hard, blunt and rough object or weapon.

**Types / Classification of Abrasion:**
1. **Scratches / linear abrasion:** Caused by horizontal or tangential friction by pointed end of weapon. Wider at starting than at ending; denuded epithelium heaps up at the end.
2. **Grazes / sliding abrasion (or brush burn or gravel rash):** Caused by horizontal or tangential friction between epithelium and some rough surface of an object, ground or weapon. Wider and deeper at the beginning; heaping of epithelium is present at the end. Most commonly in RTA.
3. **Pressure abrasion:** Caused by more or less perpendicular force on the body surface. Friction is less and is directed towards the depth of the body. Examples include ligature mark in hanging or strangulation, nail marks in throttling, and teeth bite marks.
4. **Imprint / impact or patterned abrasion:** Design and shape of weapon which causes it is left. Weapon of offence can be guessed from it (e.g., tyre mark in RTA).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 217 & Page 218

questions.text: Mention the prerequisites for starting medico-legal autopsy.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Prerequisites of Medico-Legal Autopsy:**
* **A. Requisite papers:**
  1. A copy of inquest report.
  2. A copy of chalan.
  3. A copy of death certificate (in case of hospital death).
  4. Commanding certificate of police constable who carry and identify the dead body.
* **B. Government authorized morgue.**
* **C. Natural broad day light.**
* **D. An ideal morgue/mortuary.**

**Guide Book Page:** Page 196

questions.text: What are the causes of death due to hanging?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Immediate Causes of Death in Hanging:**
1. **Asphyxia:** Ligature forces root of tongue against posterior wall of pharynx, and folds epiglottis over entrance of larynx to block airway. A weight of 15 Kg is required to block trachea.
2. **Apoplexy / venous congestion:** Jugular veins can be blocked with only pressure of 2 Kg on neck which stops cerebral circulation, causes rapid rise of venous pressure in head and unconsciousness.
3. **Combination of asphyxia and apoplexy:** Most common cause.
4. **Cerebral anemia or ischemia:** Pressure on large arteries of neck stops flow of blood in them (cerebral anemia and immediate coma).
5. **Reflex vagal inhibition (i.e., vagal shock):** Carotid sinus gets stimulated when irritated by compression and causes vagal inhibition of heart, causing it to stop.
6. **Fracture-dislocation of 2nd and 3rd cervical vertebra:** Leading to injury to medulla and upper part of spinal cord, as in case of judicial hanging.

*(Delayed causes include: Infections, aspiration pneumonia, edema of lungs/larynx, hypoxic encephalopathy, infarction of brain, cerebral abscess, and cerebral softening).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 297 & Page 298

questions.text: What do you mean by coup lesion and contre-coup lesion?
questions.answerMarkdown:
* **Coup Lesion:**
  * **Meaning:** Coup (blow, impact) means that injury is located beneath the area of impact, and results directly by the impacting force. Effects are immediate, resulting in contusions and hemorrhage.
  * **Features:**
    * Usually occurs when the head is fixed.
    * Smaller the impact area the greater is the likelihood of a coup injury.
    * *Example:* If head is fixed (e.g., when lying on the ground) and there is violent impact over the occiput, the fracture and underlying brain damage will be located beneath the site of impact.

* **Contre-Coup (Contrecoup) Lesion:**
  * **Meaning:** Contrecoup lesion means that lesion is present in an area opposite to the side of impact.
  * **Features:**
    * Usually occurs when head is free / not supported.
    * Situated on the contralateral side of the impact area.
    * Subdural or subarachnoid hemorrhage may be caused as a contre-coup lesion.
    * Sustained in falls and RTAs when moving head decelerates suddenly by hitting a hard surface.
    * *Mechanism:* Caused when moving head is suddenly decelerated by hitting a firm/hard surface. Sudden arrest of head results in brain injury which is still in motion, striking the arrested skull. Also, formation of cavity or vacuum in cranial cavity on the opposite side of impact exerts a suction effect which damages the brain.
    * *Example:* When a person falls upon the back of his head striking the ground, he may sustain brain injury at the site of impact, i.e., occipital lobes (coup injury), and a more pronounced injury to the frontal lobes (contre-coup injury).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 359 & Page 360

questions.text: What are the cardinal autopsy findings in case of death due to starvation?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Cardinal Signs of Starvation (present in chronic starvation cases):**
1. **Emaciated body with total loss of subcutaneous fat**.
2. **Scaphoid / concave shaped abdomen**.
3. **Distended gall bladder (GB) containing thick inspissated bile**.
4. **Translucent tissue paper-like intestine**.

*(Alternative / Surest signs: Enlarged GB containing thick, viscid or blackish bile; extremely translucent intestinal wall like tissue paper; all internal organs atrophied except brain).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 377 (also summarized on Page 379)

questions.text: What are the differences between burn and scald?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Difference between dry heat (burn) and moist heat (scald) injury:**

| Feature | Burn | Scald |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Cause** | Flame, hot metal | Boiling water, milk, oil etc. |
| **Site** | At or above site of contact | At or below site of contact |
| **Skin appearance** | Reddening, blister formation, charring and blackening | Reddening, blister formation, sodden and bleached |
| **Depth** | Often deep to skin or more deep | Usually less |
| **Singeing of hair** | Present | Absent |
| **Splashing** | Absent | Present |
| **Scar** | Thick | Thin |
| **Contracture** | Common | Not common |
| **Clothes** | Burnt | Not burnt |
| **Healing** | Delayed | Comparatively early |
| **Fatality** | More fatal | Less fatal |
| **ML aspects** | Suicidal, accidental, rarely homicidal | Usually accidental, occasionally homicidal |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 347

questions.text: What are the differences between fee sharing & fee splitting?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Difference between fee-sharing and fee-splitting:**

| Feature | Fee-sharing | Fee-splitting / dichotomy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition** | Sharing of fee among surgeon, assistants, nurses and bearers | Receiving or giving commission or other benefits to a colleague or manufacturer |
| **Ethics** | Ethical | Unethical |
| **Punishment** | No punishment | Warning or erasure of name |

* **Fee sharing:** Sharing of fees generally received in an operation among surgeon, his/her assistants, nurses and bearers, especially in private clinics, is called fee-sharing. It is ethical and does not constitute professional infamous conduct.
* **Fee-splitting (Dichotomy):** Receiving or giving commission or other benefits to a colleague or manufacturer or trader in drugs or appliances or a chemist or a dentist etc. It is unethical and constitutes professional infamous conduct (PIC).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 62 & Page 63

questions.text: When leading question is allowed during examination in chief part of deposition in the Court of Law? Who examine the witness?
questions.answerMarkdown:
* **Who examines the witness in examination-in-chief?**
  * Examination-in-chief is conducted by the **lawyer for the side which has summoned him**.

* **When leading question is allowed during examination-in-chief?**
  * Leading questions are allowed with the permission of the court under the following circumstances:
    1. While making introductory remarks / presenting undisputed matters (e.g., when name, occupation etc. of witness are asked).
    2. While presenting identification facts (when attention of witness is drawn for identifying person or thing).
    3. To assert memory.
    4. While giving contradictions.
    5. When a witness is declared as a hostile witness.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 26 & Page 28

questions.text: From what findings of entry wound you can say that it is of near shot range of rifled firearm injury?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Findings of Entrance Wound in Near Range (up to 1 m) of Rifled-Weapon:**
1. **Circular hole with abrasion collar** (marginal abrasion due to rubbing of the gyrating body of the bullet against inverted epidermis and heat of bullet).
2. **Absence of burning, soiling, burnt hair or carbon monoxide in tissues** (distinguishing it from contact and close range shots of 5–8 cm).

*(Contextual comparison of ranges according to the Guide Book):*
* **Close range (5–8 cm):** Circular hole with abrasion collar, flame burn on surrounding skin and hairs, soot (carbon particles) and smoke soiling, and unburnt propellant flakes.
* **Near range (up to 1 m):** Circular hole with abrasion collar; **no burning, soiling, burnt hair or monoxide**.
* **Distant range (>1 m):** Smaller, irregular hole with irregular abrasion collar; no other features.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 275 (also see Page 273 & Page 274)

questions.text: Define Medical Jurisprudence?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Medical Jurisprudence:** *(juris = law; prudential = knowledge)*
* Medical jurisprudence is the science that deals with the application of rules and regulations for the guidance of medical professionals. It deals with the relationships which have legal consequences e.g. doctor-doctor relationship, doctor-patient relationship, doctor-state relationship.
* *Or,* Medical jurisprudence deals with legal responsibilities of physician/doctor with particular reference to those arising from physician-patient relationship/doctor-patient relationship e.g. medical negligence cases, consent, rights and duties of doctors, serious professional misconduct, medical ethics etc.
* In short, medical jurisprudence deals with legal aspects of practice of medicine.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 7 & Page 8

questions.text: What do you mean by BMDC & BMA?
questions.answerMarkdown:
* **BMDC (Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council):**
  BMDC is a statutory/constitutional/legal body who adopted an ethical code for the registered medical practitioners of Bangladesh.
* **BMA (Bangladesh Medical Association):**
  BMA (Bangladesh Medical Association) is a non-government organization for all registered medical practitioners.
  * *Functions:* Tries to establish rights and privileges of registered medical practitioners.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 51 & Page 55

questions.text: Define medico-legal autopsy.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Medico-Legal Autopsy:**
* Medico-legal autopsy is made compulsory by the law in unnatural and suspicious circumstance of deaths.
* **Purposes:**
  * Purpose is to find out cause of death and help dispensation of justice, if any crime involved.
  * In most accidental deaths, ideally an autopsy is required to rule out any foul play.

*(General definition: Autopsy may be defined as an extensive and elaborate scientific examination of a dead body through and through, both externally and internally by naked eye examination and/or by magnifying glass and by dissecting each and every organ with the help of microbiological, pathological and serological examination and also by chemical analysis to find out or determine the cause, nature, manner, time passed since death, and as evidence of identification).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 192 & Page 193

questions.text: Define laceration. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Laceration:**
* **Laceration (tear / rupture):** Lacerations are tears or splits of skin, mucous membranes, muscles or internal organs produced by application of blunt force to a broad area of the body which crushed or stretched tissues beyond limits of their elasticity.

**Types / Classification of Laceration Wound:**
1. **Split lacerations:** Occurs due to crushing of skin and sub-cutaneous tissue by hard blunt weapon against bony surface. It is usually found on areas of body which have subcutaneous bones like scalp, shin of tibia and ulnar border of forearm.
2. **Stretch lacerations:** Caused by forceful frictional impact by hard blunt and rough objects; over-stretching of skin and sub-cutaneous tissue may cause laceration with flapping of skin etc. It is usually seen in run-over motor vehicles.
3. **Avulsion / shearing lacerations:** In this type of laceration there is separation of skin from underlying tissue by shearing force delivered at an acute angle. Such laceration is caused by vehicles in RTA.
   * *Flaying:* Shearing and grinding force by a weight (e.g. lorry wheel passing over a limb) may produce separation (avulsion) of skin from underlying tissues over a relatively large area.
4. **Cut laceration:** This is caused by not-so-sharp edged heavy or moderately heavy instruments, which cause a deep and wide cut over body tissues. They are often seen in chop wound.
5. **Tears:** Tearing of skin & tissues can occur from impact by or against irregular or semi-sharp objects, such as door handle of car. May be caused by blows, broken glass or fall over rough projected object.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 227 & Page 228

questions.text: What are the causes of RTAs?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Causes of RTA (Road Traffic Accident):**
* a. Fault of victim.
* b. Fault of driver.
* c. Fault of vehicle.
* d. Fault of another vehicle, not involved in crime.
* e. Bad road condition.
* f. Wrong signaling.
* g. More than one of above causes.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 367

questions.text: What are the differences between somatic death and molecular death?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Difference between Somatic and Molecular Death:**

| Feature | Somatic death | Molecular/cellular death |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition** | Complete and irreversible stoppage of tripod of life | Death of cells and tissues individually |
| **Time of occurrence** | Immediately | 3–6 hrs after somatic death (usually 1–2 hours) |
| **Precedence** | Precede molecular death | Follow somatic death |
| **Organ transplantation** | Organ can be removed for transplantation | Organ can’t be removed for transplantation |
| **Response to electric stimuli, ECG, EEG** | Yes | No |
| **Gaping of wound** | Yes | No |
| **Blister formation in burn** | Yes | No |
| **Suspended animation** | May be confused with it | No chance of confusion |
| **Sign of death** | Unreliable sign | Reliable sign |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 140 & Page 141

questions.text: Mention differences between hanging and strangulation?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Difference between Hanging and Strangulation:**

| Feature | Hanging | Strangulation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ligature mark** | Oblique, non-continuous, high-up | Transverse, complete, low |
| **Base of ligature mark** | Pale, hard, parchment-like | Soft and reddish |
| **Abrasions and ecchymoses around edges of ligature** | Not common | Common |
| **Bruising of neck muscle** | Less common | More common |
| **Neck** | Stretched and elongated | Not stretched and elongated |
| **Subcutaneous tissue** | White, hard & glistening under mark | Ecchymosed under mark |
| **Fracture of hyoid bone** | May occur | Un-common |
| **Fracture of thyroid cartilage** | Less common | More common |
| **Fracture of larynx & trachea** | Rare | May be found |
| **Emphysematous bullae on lungs** | Not present | Very common |
| **Damage of carotid arteries** | May be seen | Rare |
| **Signs of asphyxia** | Less marked | Well marked |
| **Face** | Usually pale, petechiae aren't common | Congested, marked with petechiae |
| **Tongue** | Swelling & protrusion less marked | Swelling & protrusion more marked |
| **Saliva** | Often runs out of mouth | Absent |
| **Bleeding from nose, mouth, ears** | Not common | Common |
| **Involuntary discharge of feces & urine** | Less common | More common |
| **Involuntary discharge of seminal fluid** | More common | Less common |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 309

questions.text: Mention the lung findings during autopsy in case of infanticide.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Autopsy Lung Findings in Infanticide (Live-Born / Respiration vs. Dead-Born / Stillborn):**

| Feature | Respiration / Live-Born Lung | Unrespirated / Stillborn Lung |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Volume** | Large, covers the heart; enormous increase in volume | Normal or small; does not cover heart |
| **Weight** | Weight doubles (1/35 of body weight) | 1/70 of body weight |
| **Margins** | Rounded | Sharp |
| **Consistency** | Soft, spongy, elastic, and crepitant | Dense, firm, non-crepitant (liver-like) |
| **Color** | Mottled or marbled in appearance (pale pink / light red) | Uniformly dark red, reddish-brown or bluish-red |
| **Air vesicles** | Inflated | Not inflated |
| **Section** | Abundant frothy blood exudates on section | Little frothless blood exudates on pressure |
| **Flotation (Hydrostatic / Raygat’s test)** | Expanded whole lung and its cut pieces float in water | Whole lung and cut parts sink in water |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 505 & Page 508

questions.text: How will you identify entry wound close shot range rifled firearm injury?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Findings of Entrance Wound in Close Range (5–8 cm) of Rifled-Weapon:**
* a. **Circular hole with abrasion collar** (marginal abrasion due to rubbing of the gyrating body of the bullet against inverted epidermis and heat of bullet).
* b. **Flame burn** on surrounding skin and hairs (singeing of hair).
* c. **Soot (carbon particles) and smoke soiling** (blackening).
* d. **Unburnt propellant flakes** embedded in the skin (tattooing / powder peppering).
* e. **Little or no monoxide in tissues** (local cherry red discoloration).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 274 & Page 275

questions.text: How will you estimate 3% burn?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Estimation of 3% Burn:**
* **By Palm Rule:**
  * According to the Guide Book, **"One palm area is equal to 1% of burn"**.
  * Therefore, a burned surface area equivalent to **three (3) palms of the patient's hand** is estimated as a **3% burn**.
* *(In relation to Wallace's Rule of 9's: The perineum/genitalia is 1% of total body surface area, meaning an area equal to three times the perineum also equals 3%).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 339 & Page 340

questions.text: Define inquest? Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Inquest:**
* **Inquest:** Inquest is a preliminary investigation or inquiry into the cause of any sudden, unnatural and suspicious death.
* *Or,* Inquest is investigation into the cause of death in cases of sudden, unnatural and suspicious deaths conducted by the legal authorities.
* *Or,* Inquest is defined as the preliminary inquiry into the cause of sudden, suspicious and unnatural death, which is apparently not due to natural causes.

**Types of Inquest:**
1. **Police inquest** *(most common)*
2. **Magistrate inquest**
3. **Coroner inquest**
4. **Medical examiner system** *(best method)*
5. **Procurator fiscal**

*(Note: In Bangladesh and India, Police inquest and Magistrate inquest are practiced).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 12 & Page 13

questions.text: What do you mean by Medical etiquette? Give its example.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Medical Etiquette:**
* **Definition:** Medical etiquette deals with the conventional laws of courtesy observed between the members of the medical profession.
* *Or,* Medical etiquette actually means the sense of courtesy and mutual respect which should govern the conduct and relationship among the members of the medical profession.

**Examples of Medical Etiquette:**
1. A doctor should not criticize the professional ability of another doctor while dealing with a patient.
2. A doctor should behave with his colleagues as he would have them behave with himself (*"My colleagues will be my sisters and brothers"*).
3. Taking proper consultation when needed, and providing gratuitous service to a physician and their family without taking fees.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 8 & Page 49

questions.text: Define drowning. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Drowning:**
* **Drowning:** Drowning is a form of asphyxia due to aspiration of fluid/liquid into air passages caused by submersion in water or other fluid. *(Submersion of only mouth and nasal openings by any means is sufficient to produce drowning).*

**Types of Drowning:**
1. **Dry drowning** (Type-I)
2. **Wet drowning / primary drowning** (Type-II):
   * a. Fresh water drowning (Type-IIA)
   * b. Salt water drowning (Type-IIB)
3. **Shallow water drowning**
4. **Secondary drowning / post-immersion syndrome / near drowning**
5. **Immersion syndrome / hydrocution / submersion inhibition**

*(Alternative classification into Typical / Wet drowning and Atypical drowning: dry drowning, shallow water drowning, secondary drowning, and immersion syndrome).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 317

questions.text: Mention the common sites of concealed punctured wound.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Sites of Concealed Punctured Wound:**
1. **Fontanelle of newborn** *(anterior fontanelle before ossification; sagittal sinus is mainly injured)*
2. **Nape of the neck**
3. **Soft palate**
4. **Nostrils** *(nasal aperture)*
5. **Fornix of upper eyelids, medial canthus of eye**
6. **Under fold of female breast**
7. **Axilla** *(fold of axilla)*
8. **Vagina**
9. **Rectum**

*(Medico-legal importance: These injuries are undetectable unless searched carefully, and are always homicidal).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 239

questions.text: What do you mean by negative autopsy?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Negative Autopsy:**
* **Definition:** When gross and microscopic examination, toxicological analysis report and laboratory investigations fail to reveal a cause of death, it is termed as negative autopsy.
* **Rate:** The rate of negative autopsy is about 2–5%.

**Causes of Negative Autopsy:**
1. Inadequate history.
2. Inadequate external examination.
3. Inadequate or improper internal examination.
4. Insufficient lab examinations.
5. Lack of toxicological analysis.
6. Lack of doctor's training.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 204 & Page 205

questions.text: What are the effect heat and cold to the body?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Effects of Exposure to Extreme Heat:**
1. **General effects:**
   * a. Heat stroke / heat hyperpyrexia (rectal temperature >41°C with delirium, convulsions, coma).
   * b. Heat exhaustion / heat collapse / heat syncope (peripheral circulatory collapse without increase in body temperature).
   * c. Heat cramps / miner’s cramps (painful spasms of muscles due to water and salt depletion).
   * d. Sunburn / heat rash.
2. **Local effects:**
   * a. Burn (dry heat injury).
   * b. Scald (moist heat injury).

**Effects of Exposure to Extreme Cold:**
1. **General effects:**
   * a. Hypothermia (body temperature fall <35°C, ending in cardiac arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation, coma, and failure of vital centers).
   * b. Immersion syndrome / cold shock.
2. **Local effects:**
   * a. Frost bite (infarction, blistering, and necrosis of peripheral digits, nose, ears).
   * b. Trench foot / immersion foot (due to prolonged exposure to damp cold above freezing point).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 332 & Page 335

questions.text: Mention the types of intracranial haemorrhage.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Types of Intracranial Hemorrhage:**
1. **Extradural or epidural hemorrhage (EDH):** Hemorrhage in the extradural space between the skull and dura mater (usually from rupture of the middle meningeal vessels).
2. **Subdural hemorrhage (SDH):** Hemorrhage beneath the dura mater into the subdural space (usually from rupture of bridging/communicating veins).
3. **Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH):** Hemorrhage into the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia mater (from head trauma or rupture of berry aneurysms).
4. **Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH):** Bleeding inside the substance of the brain itself.
5. **Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH):** Hemorrhage inside the ventricular system of the brain.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 361

questions.text: Mention the differential diagnosis of cadaveric spasm.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differential Diagnoses of Cadaveric Spasm (Conditions Simulating Rigidity / Muscle Stiffening):**
1. **Rigor mortis:** Gradual stiffening of muscles following molecular death, preceded by a phase of primary flaccidity, involving all muscles progressively.
2. **Heat stiffening (Heat coagulation):** Rigidity caused by exposure to high temperatures (>65°C) due to denaturation and coagulation of muscle proteins.
3. **Cold stiffening (Freezing):** Stiffening produced when the body is exposed to freezing temperatures (<4°C) due to frozen fluids and fats in tissues.
4. **Gas stiffening:** Stiffening produced by the accumulation and distension of putrefactive gases within body tissues during decomposition.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 174, Page 175 & Page 189

questions.text: During autopsy, from lung findings how can you say it was a case of live birth?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Autopsy Lung Findings Indicating Live Birth (Respirated Lungs):**
1. **Volume:** Enormous increase in volume; expanded lungs completely cover the pericardial sac / heart.
2. **Weight:** Weight of lungs is doubled (approximately 1/35 of total body weight, compared to 1/70 in stillborn).
3. **Margin:** Margins are rounded and blunt (rather than sharp).
4. **Consistency:** Soft, spongy, elastic, and crepitant to touch (air-filled vesicles crackle on pressure).
5. **Color:** Mottled or marbled in appearance (pale pink / light red), rather than uniformly dark reddish-brown.
6. **On Sectioning:** Abundant frothy blood exudates from the cut surface on gentle pressure.
7. **Hydrostatic Test (Raygat’s Test):** Whole lung and all its cut pieces (12 to 20 pieces) float buoyantly in water, even after firm compression to expel tidal air (due to retained residual air).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 505 & Page 508

questions.text: How can you sure that the entry wound is due to suicidal firearm injury?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Findings Confirming Entry Wound Due to Suicidal Firearm Injury:**
1. **Site of entry wound:** Situated over accessible, elective sites of the body:
   * Temple (60%, usually right temple in right-handed individuals).
   * Center of forehead.
   * Roof of mouth.
   * Midline behind the chin.
   * Left side / front of the chest over the precordial region.
2. **Range / Shot distance:** Wound is of **contact** or **very close range** (shows muzzle impression, singeing/burning of hair and skin, intense blackening by smoke soot, and powder tattooing/peppering).
3. **Direction of track:** Directed upward and backward.
4. **Number of wounds:** Usually single entry wound (rarely a second if the first was not instantly fatal).
5. **Presumptive supportive evidence:**
   * Weapon firmly grasped in the hand in **cadaveric spasm** (undoubted proof of suicide).
   * Powder residue / blackening present on the hand pressing the trigger.
   * Absence of struggle marks or defense wounds elsewhere on the body.
   * Exposed/undressed site of injury or weapon held beneath clothing.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 278 & Page 279

questions.text: Define evidence. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Evidence:**
* **Evidence:** Evidence means any statement in relation to a matter or fact under inquiry or a document or something, for the inspection of the court.

**Types of Evidence:**
* **A. Oral evidence:**
  1. Direct evidence.
  2. Indirect/circumstantial evidence.
  3. Hearsay evidence.
* **B. Documentary evidence:**
  1. Medical certificate.
  2. Medico-legal report.
  3. Dying declaration.
  4. Dying deposition.

*(Other definitions of evidence in law include Primary evidence, Secondary evidence, Material evidence, and Prima facie evidence).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 33 & Page 34

questions.text: Define abrasion mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Abrasion:**
* **Abrasion:** Abrasion is damage or destruction of superficial epithelial covering of skin (epidermis) or mucus membrane, due to impact (mostly frictions) with hard, blunt and rough object or weapon.
* *Or,* Abrasion is temporary loss of superficial epithelial covering of skin (epidermis) or mucus membrane, due to forcible friction of body surface against hard, blunt and rough object or weapon.

**Types of Abrasion:**
1. **Scratches / linear abrasion:** Caused by horizontal or tangential friction by pointed end of weapon. Wider at starting than at ending; denuded epithelium heaps up at the end.
2. **Grazes / sliding abrasion (or brush burn or gravel rash):** Caused by horizontal or tangential friction between epithelium and some rough surface of an object, ground or weapon. Wider and deeper at the beginning; heaping of epithelium is present at the end. Most commonly in RTA.
3. **Pressure abrasion:** Caused by more or less perpendicular force on the body surface. Friction is less and is directed towards the depth of the body (e.g., ligature mark in hanging or strangulation, nail marks in throttling, and teeth bite marks).
4. **Imprint / impact or patterned abrasion:** Design and shape of weapon which causes it is left. Weapon of offence can be guessed from it (e.g., tyre mark in RTA).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 217 & Page 218

questions.text: Define hanging. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Hanging:**
* **Hanging:** Hanging is a form of asphyxial death, which is caused by suspension of body by a ligature that encircles neck and constricting force being weight of whole body or weight of head alone.

**Types / Classification of Hanging:**
* **A. According to position of knot:**
  * a. **Typical hanging:** Knot is present in nape of neck (not very common).
  * b. **Atypical hanging:** Knot is present in any site other than nape of neck (common).
* **B. According to degree of suspension:**
  * a. **Complete hanging:** No part of body touches ground.
  * b. **Partial hanging:** Some part of body touches ground.
* **C. According to ML importance / manner of hanging:**
  * a. Suicidal hanging *(most common)*.
  * b. Homicidal hanging.
  * c. Accidental hanging.
* **D. According to time related to death:**
  * a. Ante-mortem hanging.
  * b. Post-mortem hanging.
* **E. According to length of ligature material:**
  * a. Long drop.
  * b. Short drop.
  * c. Intermediate.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 295 & Page 296

questions.text: What are the functions of BM&DC?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Functions of BM&DC (Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council):**

* **A. Academic:**
  1. Prescribe course curriculum and syllabus for under-graduate medical and dental education.
  2. Maintain standard of undergraduate medical and dental education.
  3. Prescribe standards of post-graduate medical and dental education for guidance of public universities of Bangladesh.
  4. Prescribing the conditions for admission to courses of training.

* **B. Administrative:**
  1. Give registration to newly passed MBBS and BDS doctors.
  2. Maintenance of registers of medical and dental practitioners.
  3. Recognize local medical and dental qualifications.
  4. Recognize foreign medical and dental qualifications.
  5. Issue warning notice or erasure (temporary or permanent) of name for PIC.
  6. Action against registered practitioners for using false title etc.
  7. Action against persons not registered under the act.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 52

questions.text: What are the criminal causes of infanticide?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Criminal Causes of Infant Death or Neonatal Death:**

* **A. Acts of commission:** (Done positively to cause the death of the infant)
  1. **Suffocation.**
  2. **Throttling or strangulation.**
  3. **Blunt head injury** (rare).
  4. **Fractures and dislocation of cervical vertebrae.**
  5. **Wounds** e.g. stabs, incised wounds, cut-throat etc.
  6. **Drowning** — rare, but may be used as a mode of disposal.
  7. **Burning** — rare, but may be used as a mode of disposal.
  8. **Poison** (rare).

* **B. Acts of omission or neglect:** (Failure to take ordinary precautions to save child after birth)
  1. Failure to provide proper assistance during labor may cause death by suffocation or head injury.
  2. Failure to tie the cord after cutting/dividing and causing death by hemorrhage.
  3. Failure to clear air-passages which may be obstructed by amniotic fluid or mucus.
  4. Failure to protect the child from exposure to heat or cold.
  5. Failure to supply the child with proper food.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 510 (also Page 501)

questions.text: Mention the changes that take place in human body after death.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Changes After Death / Signs of Death:**

* **A. Immediate signs/changes (Somatic death):** (After 3 minutes)
  * a. Stoppage of function of nervous system / insensibility and loss of voluntary power:
    * Complete insensibility.
    * Loss of EEG rhythm.
  * b. Stoppage/cessation of respiration or respiratory arrest.
  * c. Stoppage/cessation of circulation or circulatory arrest.

* **B. Early signs/changes (Cellular death):** (12–24 hours)
  * a. Pallor and loss of skin elasticity.
  * b. Changes in eye (loss of corneal reflex, opacity of cornea, fall in IOP, *tache noire*, Kevorkian sign / trucking of retinal vessels).
  * c. Primary flaccidity of muscles.
  * d. Cooling of body (*algor mortis*).
  * e. Postmortem lividity/staining (*hypostasis* / *livor mortis*).
  * f. Rigor mortis / postmortem rigidity.

* **C. Late signs/changes (Decomposition and decay):** (After 24 hours)
  * a. Putrefaction.
  * b. Adipocere formation.
  * c. Mummification.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 159

questions.text: Mention the character of pedestrian injury in road traffic accidents?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Injuries of Pedestrians in RTA:**

* **1. Primary impact injuries:**
  * Due to first impact of vehicle on victim. Part of body involved and injuries depend upon relative position of vehicle and victim.
  * These injuries are very much important to detect the offending vehicle; they may bear the design of part of vehicle causing injuries in the form of **imprint abrasion or patterned bruise**.
  * Typically presents as **bumper injuries** (fractures of tibia and fibula, often compound, and extensive soft tissue damage on the legs).

* **2. Secondary impact injuries:**
  * Due to further injuries caused by vehicle.
  * Usually victim is thrown forward and falls on vehicle (radiator, bonnet, or windscreen) and run over by vehicle.
  * **Avulsion laceration** is the most frequent injury caused due to run over by the vehicle; tyre tread marks may be imprinted on the skin.

* **3. Secondary injuries / tertiary injuries:**
  * Injuries caused by victim striking objects such as the ground/roadway.
  * Injuries may be any of hard blunt force injuries: **graze abrasions** (brush burns/gravel rash) and **stretch lacerations** are commonest. Sand, soil, or gravel embedded on injuries help link to the place of occurrence.

* **Characteristic injuries summary:**
  * Abrasion, bruise, laceration etc.
  * Avulsed lacerations of the limbs.
  * Bumper fracture.
  * Crushing of the head.
  * Blunt trauma to chest or abdomen (fracture of ribs, fracture of hip bone, rupture of liver/spleen, lungs, heart).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 367, Page 368 & Page 369

questions.text: How can you differentiate ante-mortem blister from postmortem blister?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Difference between Ante-Mortem and Post-Mortem Blister:**

| Feature | Ante-Mortem Blister | Post-Mortem Blister |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Surroundings** | Surrounded by red-ring (vital reaction / line of redness) | Not so (no red ring) |
| **Base** | Red, inflamed with raised papillae | Dry, hard, horny and yellow |
| **Content** | Serous fluid containing abundant albumin and chlorides | Air only, or may contain very small quantity of serum with a trace of albumen |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 345

questions.text: Why choking is done within the inner aspect of the distal 7.5 to 10.0 cm of the barrel of shot gun?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Choking:**
* **Choking:** Choking is the slight constriction of terminal few centimeters (7.5–10 cm) of bore near muzzle end in some smooth-bored guns.

**Why Choking is Done / Advantages & Importance:**
1. **Decreases the rate of dispersion of shots** (keeps pellets grouped closer together over longer flight).
2. **Increases accuracy of shot.**
3. **Increases the effective range of shot.**
4. **Increases force/velocity of projectiles.**

**Guide Book Page:** Page 269

questions.text: How can you differentiate live birth from dead born during autopsy?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Difference between Dead-Born Child and Live-Born Child (Autopsy Findings):**

| Feature | Dead-Born Child | Live-Born Child |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Chest** | Flat | Arched or drummed shaped |
| **Rigor mortis** | Present *(at delivery)* | Absent *(at birth)* |
| **Maceration** | Present | Absent |
| **Mummification** | Present | Absent |
| **Diaphragm** | Level of 4th or 5th rib | Level of 6th or 7th rib |
| **Lung weight** | 1/70 of body weight | 1/35 of body weight (weight doubles) |
| **Lung volume** | Normal or small (does not cover heart) | Large, covers the heart |
| **Lung margin** | Sharp | Rounded |
| **Lung consistency** | Dense, firm, non-crepitant (liver-like) | Soft, spongy, elastic, crepitant |
| **Lung color** | Uniformly reddish-brown or bluish red | Mottled or marbled appearance (pale pink) |
| **Air vesicles** | Not inflated | Inflated |
| **Cut section of lung** | Little frothless blood exudates on pressure | Abundant frothy blood exudates on section |
| **Hydrostatic test (Raygat's test)** | Whole and parts sink in water | Expanded or whole lung floats in water |
| **Stomach & bowel (Breslau's test)** | Nothing present (sinks in water) | Air, fluid, milk or food may present (floats) |
| **Middle ear (Wredin's test)** | Contains gelatinous connective tissue | Contains air |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 508 (with reference to Page 504 & Page 505)
