questions.text: Mention the causes of death due to drowning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Causes of Death in Drowning:**
1. **Asphyxia:** Due to inhalation and aspiration of fluid filling the bronchial tree and alveolar spaces, blocking air exchange.
2. **Ventricular Fibrillation / Acute Heart Failure:** In **fresh water drowning**, massive hemodilution (blood volume increases by up to 50–72%) with hemolysis, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia precipitates fatal ventricular arrhythmias within 4–5 minutes.
3. **Severe Pulmonary Edema & Hypoxia:** In **salt water drowning**, hypertonic water draws fluid out of circulation into alveolar spaces, causing severe pulmonary edema, hemoconcentration, and death from anoxia within 8–12 minutes.
4. **Laryngeal Spasm (Dry Drowning):** Inrush of water into the nasopharynx or larynx triggers intense reflex laryngeal spasm, closing the airway without water entering the lungs (10–20% of cases).
5. **Vagal Inhibition (Immersion Syndrome / Hydrocution):** Cold water striking the surface of the body, epigastrium, or entering the ear/nasal passages stimulates mucosal nerve endings causing reflex vagal cardiac arrest.
6. **Exhaustion:** Physical exhaustion while struggling in water.
7. **Trauma / Secondary Injuries:** Striking submerged rocks, harbor pilings, or boat propellers causing fatal skull fracture or visceral rupture.
8. **Secondary Drowning Complications:** Hypoxic encephalopathy, adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), bronchopneumonia, or metabolic acidosis hours to days after rescue.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 318, Page 319 & Page 325

questions.text: What are the differences between anti-mortem wound from post-mortem wound?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Ante-Mortem and Post-Mortem Wounds:**

| Feature | Ante-Mortem Wound | Post-Mortem Wound |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Edges / Margins** | Swollen, everted, retracted, gaping, and inflamed | Closely approximated, non-gaping, and flat |
| **Hemorrhage** | Profuse, arterial; deep staining of surrounding tissues | Slight or absent; mainly venous oozing |
| **Arterial Spurting** | Present; blood may spurt over clothes or surroundings | Completely absent |
| **Extravasation of Blood** | Staining of wound edges by extravasated RBCs which **cannot be washed away** with water | Surface blood staining can be **easily removed by washing** |
| **Coagulation / Clotting** | Firm, tenacious, dark, adherent clots tangled in fibrin | Soft, friable "currant-jelly" clots or no clotting |
| **Vital Reaction** | **Present** (capillary dilation, inflammatory cellular infiltration, fibrin formation) | **Absent** |
| **Enzymatic Activity** | Increased histochemical enzymatic activity (esterases, ATPases) at wound margins | No increase or diminished enzyme activity |
| **Healing Signs** | Scab formation, granulation tissue, or cicatrization may be seen | Completely absent |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 261 & Page 262

questions.text: How will you give your opinion after autopsy in case of OPC poisoning?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Autopsy Opinions in a Suspected Case of OPC (Organo-Phosphorus Compound) Poisoning:**

* **Primary / Preliminary Opinion:**
  * *"Opinion as to the cause of death is kept pending (or deferred) until receipt of the report of the Chief Chemical Examiner on the preserved viscera."*

* **Final Opinion:**
  * *"Considering the post-mortem examination findings and the chemical analysis report of the preserved viscera, I am of the opinion that death was due to asphyxia as a result of Organo-Phosphorus Compound (OPC) poisoning, which was ante-mortem in nature."*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 199, Page 552 & Page 708

questions.text: How will you differentiate incise wound from heat rupture?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between an Incised Wound and Heat Rupture:**

| Feature | Incised Wound | Heat Rupture |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Causative Factor** | Mechanical violence by a sharp-cutting weapon (knife, razor) | Intense dry heat causing cooking, shrinkage, and splitting of charred tissues |
| **Common Sites** | Any accessible part of the body | Extensor surfaces of limbs, over flexures of joints, and lower abdomen |
| **Edges / Margins** | Clean-cut, sharp, well-defined, and everted | Irregular, ragged, jagged, and charred |
| **Tissue Bridges / Deep Structures** | Completely absent (all tissues sharply and cleanly divided) | **Intact blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue fibers span across the split** |
| **Bleeding & Extravasation** | Profuse bleeding with extravasation and clotted blood in the wound | **No bleeding, no clots, and no extravasation** (heat coagulates blood inside vessels) |
| **Vital Reaction** | Line of redness and inflammatory changes present | **Absent** (pure post-mortem thermal artefact) |
| **Surrounding Skin** | Healthy, normal skin | Burned, roasted, charred, or covered with heat blisters |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 231 & Page 345

questions.text: What do you mean by partial hanging?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Partial Hanging:**
* **Partial / Incomplete Hanging:** Partial or incomplete hanging is a variety of hanging in which some part of the body, especially the lower part of the body, is in touch with the ground.

**Salient Features of Partial Hanging:**
* **A.** Some part of the body touches the ground (e.g., feet, toes, knees, or buttocks resting on the floor or bed).
* **B.** The constricting force is only the weight of part of the body (the head or head and upper body), not the weight of the entire body.
* **C.** Congestive features are more pronounced, and petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots) are typically more marked.
* **D. Medico-legal Importance:** Partial hanging is **almost always suicidal** in nature (accidental is very rare; homicidal is virtually impossible unless the victim is drugged, intoxicated, or physically overpowered).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 301 (also Page 295)

questions.text: Mention the modes and manner of death.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**1. Mode of Death:**
* **Definition:** The term mode of death refers to the first failure of a vital system which initiates death.
* **Types / Modes of Death (Bichat's Classification):**
  * a. **Asphyxia:** Failure of the respiratory system.
  * b. **Syncope:** Failure of the circulatory system.
  * c. **Coma:** Failure of the nervous system.

**2. Manner of Death:**
* **Definition:** Manner of death indicates the circumstances under which the person died, or the design of how the cause of death came into action.
* **Types / Manners of Death:**
  * **A. Natural death:** If death occurs exclusively from natural disease or aging.
  * **B. Unnatural / Violent death:** If death occurs exclusively from injury, violence, or poison, or is hastened due to injury in a person suffering from disease:
    1. **Suicidal:** Death intentionally self-inflicted.
    2. **Homicidal:** Death resulting from the deliberate action of another.
    3. **Accidental:** Death as the result of an unintended environmental mishap or influence.
    4. **Undetermined or unexplained**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 146 & Page 148

questions.text: What are the characters of suicidal cut throat injury?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Characteristics of a Suicidal Cut Throat Wound:**
1. **Situation / Site:** Situated on the front and left side of the neck (rarely on both sides) in a right-handed person.
2. **Level:** Placed high up in the neck, **above the thyroid cartilage**.
3. **Direction:** Directed **obliquely downwards from left to right** (in a right-handed person).
4. **Hesitation Cuts (Tentative Cuts):** Presence of small, shallow, tentative cuts at the beginning of the main wound on the left side.
5. **Tailing:** Present at the terminal end on the right side of the neck (shallow scratch as the weapon is lifted off).
6. **Edges:** Somewhat ragged due to multiple shallow incisions over the same line.
7. **Severity & Depth:** Generally less severe; usually one or two deep cuts, shallow at origin and termination.
8. **Blood Vessels:** Large deep vessels (e.g., carotid artery) usually escape injury (protected behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle).
9. **Blood Trickling:** Blood trickles straight down over the front of the neck, chest, and abdomen in a standing or sitting posture.
10. **Defense Wounds:** **Completely absent** on hands, wrists, or forearms.
11. **Circumstances:** Quiet, secluded place, often in front of a mirror; weapon found at the scene or grasped in **cadaveric spasm**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 234 & Page 235

questions.text: Define lucid interval.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Lucid Interval:**
* **In Head Injury:**
  * The lucid interval is the state of mental clearness or normal consciousness between two states of unconsciousness in a case of head injury.
  * *(Typically seen in extradural hemorrhage [EDH] resulting from rupture of the middle meningeal artery)*.
* **In Insanity (Forensic Psychiatry):**
  * Lucid interval is defined as a period in the course of mental illness / insanity during which there is complete cessation or disappearance of symptoms of insanity, and the person is considered legally and clinically of sound mind (*compos mentis*).

**Medico-Legal Importance:**
1. **In head injury:** A patient discharged during the lucid interval may suddenly lapse into coma and die at home, potentially raising charges of medical negligence.
2. **In insanity:** During a lucid interval, the individual can validly make a will (testamentary capacity), enter into a contract, manage property, give valid evidence in court, and is held legally responsible for any criminal act committed.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 363 & Page 391

questions.text: What is choking in case of firearm? Mention its importance.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Choking:**
* **Choking:** Choking is the slight constriction or narrowing of the terminal few centimeters (7.5 to 10 cm) of the bore near the muzzle end in some smooth-bored guns (shotguns).

**Importance / Advantages of Choking:**
1. **Decreases shot dispersion:** Prevents rapid spreading and scattering of the pellets as they leave the barrel.
2. **Increases accuracy:** Keeps the shot charge compact, ensuring a denser pattern on the target.
3. **Increases the effective range:** Extends the killing range of the firearm.
4. **Increases pellet velocity and striking force:** Concentrates the kinetic energy of the pellets.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 269

questions.text: What are the differences between death due to starvation & cholera?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Death Due to Starvation and Cholera:**

| Feature | Starvation | Cholera |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Causative Organism** | No organism | *Vibrio cholerae* |
| **Epidemic Pattern** | Not epidemic | Spreads in epidemic form |
| **Intercurrent Disease** | Present (e.g., anemia, malaria, pneumonia, TB) | Usually absent |
| **Stool** | Watery | Typical "rice-water" stools |
| **Amount of Body Fat** | **Marked deprivation / complete absence of body fat** | **No deprivation of body fat** |
| **Loss of Body Weight** | **Marked loss (> 40% of total body weight)** | Not so marked (rapid dehydration, but no muscle wasting) |
| **Gall Bladder (PM Finding)** | **Distended, contains thick, dark, inspissated bile** | Normal size and normal bile content |
| **Stomach (PM Finding)** | Small, contracted, wall thin, mucosal membrane bile-stained | Not shrunken or bile-stained |
| **Heart (PM Finding)** | Small, shows brown atrophy | Normal |
| **Skeleton (PM Finding)** | Demineralized, bony prominences starkly visible | Normal |
| **Edema** | Hunger edema appears first on face, then extends to limbs | No edema |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 379 & Page 380

questions.text: What are the precautions you will take during lightning?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Precautionary Steps to Avoid Lightning Stroke:**
1. **Stay Indoors:** Do not go outside (remain indoors) when thunderstorms are nearby.
2. **Seek Safe Shelter:** If thunder is heard, immediately move inside a fully enclosed, sturdy building or a hard-topped metal vehicle with windows rolled up.
3. **Avoid Unsafe Structures:** Sheds, picnic shelters, tents, and open covered porches do **not** protect against lightning.
4. **Indoor Hazards:**
   * Avoid standing near open doors, windows, and indoor fireplaces.
   * Do not touch electrical equipment, wiring, or corded phones (cordless and cell phones are safe).
   * Do not take a bath or shower (avoid contact with plumbing fixtures).
5. **If Caught Outdoors Without Sturdy Shelter:**
   * Seek shelter in a cave, ground depression, or at the foot of a cliff.
   * **Avoid isolated tall trees** (shelter may be taken among shorter trees near taller ones).
   * Stay away from hilltops, open fields, wire/metallic fences, and bodies of water.
   * Avoid handling inflammable fuels or metallic objects.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 354

questions.text: What are the differences between fee-splitting and fee-sharing?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Fee-Sharing and Fee-Splitting:**

| Feature | Fee-Sharing | Fee-Splitting (Dichotomy) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition** | Sharing of professional fees among the surgeon, assistants, anesthetist, nurses, and staff involved in an operation | Receiving or giving commission, cuts, or other financial benefits to a colleague, manufacturer, chemist, or diagnostic center |
| **Ethical Status** | **Ethical** and accepted medical practice | **Unethical**; constitutes **Professional Infamous Conduct (PIC)** |
| **Disciplinary Action** | No punishment or disciplinary action | Warning or erasure of doctor's name from register by BMDC (Professional death sentence) |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 62 & Page 63

questions.text: What are the incisions you will give to the scalp & skull during autopsy?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Incisions Given to the Scalp and Skull During Autopsy:**

* **1. Incision of the Scalp (Coronal Incision):**
  * A **coronal incision** is made across the scalp.
  * It starts from the **mastoid process behind one ear**, passes **over the vertex**, and extends down to the **mastoid process behind the opposite ear**.
  * The anterior flap of the scalp is reflected forwards down to the level of the supraorbital ridges (protecting the eyeballs).
  * The posterior flap is reflected backwards down to a point just below the external occipital protuberance, fully exposing the calvarium.

* **2. Incision / Opening of the Skull (Removal of the Calvarium):**
  * The exposed temporal muscles and pericranium are incised and scraped away along the line of the intended saw cut.
  * The skull cap (calvarium) is removed by **sawing in a circular or V-shaped (wedge) cut**:
    * The cut passes horizontally around the forehead about 2 to 2.5 cm above the orbital margins.
    * It extends laterally above the ear attachments and passes backwards to meet at the external occipital protuberance.
  * Sawing is carried only through the outer table and diploë; the inner table is cracked using a chisel and hammer to prevent lacerating the underlying dura mater and brain.
  * The skull cap is then levered off with a T-chisel.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 197 & Page 198

questions.text: Under what condition leading question is allowed during examination in chief part of deposition in the Court of Law? Who ask the question?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**1. Who Asks the Question:**
* In examination-in-chief, the questions are asked by the **lawyer of the party who called or summoned the witness** (e.g., the Public Prosecutor / Government Pleader).

**2. Conditions When Leading Questions are Allowed in Examination-in-Chief:**
A leading question (one that suggests the desired answer) is generally prohibited in examination-in-chief, but the court may permit it in the following situations:
1. **Introductory or Undisputed Matters:** Questions relating to the witness’s name, age, residence, medical qualification, and official designation.
2. **Matters of Identification:** When drawing the witness's attention to identify an accused person, an exhibit, or a weapon of offense.
3. **To Refresh or Assert Memory:** To direct the witness's attention to an already established fact or previous official report.
4. **Points of Contradiction:** When seeking contradictions to previous depositions.
5. **Hostile Witness:** When the court formally declares the witness **hostile** (unfriendly or adverse to the party that called him).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 26 & Page 28

questions.text: What is strangulation? Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Strangulation:**
* **Strangulation:** Strangulation is a form of asphyxia which is caused by constriction of the neck by means of a ligature or by some other means, without suspending the body of the victim, where the constricting force is applied from outside and is not the weight of the body or head of the victim.

**Types / Methods of Strangulation:**
* **A. Strangulation Proper:**
  * **Ligature strangulation:** Constriction of the neck by a ligature.
* **B. Manual Strangulation / Throttling:**
  * Constriction of the neck by the human hands.
* **C. Mechanical Strangulation:**
  * a. **Garroting:** Compression by a special type of ligature or twisting cord/stick.
  * b. **Mugging:** Compression by the crook of the elbow (elbow bent) or knee bent.
  * c. **Bansdolla:** Compression of the neck between two bamboo sticks (one in front and another behind, or one against the ground).
* **D. Palmar Strangulation:**
  * Compression of the throat using the base of the palm.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 304 (also Page 308)

questions.text: Define professional secrecy. Give example.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Professional Secrecy:**
* **Professional Secrecy:** Professional secrecy is an implied term of contract between a doctor and his patients whereby a doctor is obliged to keep secret, all that he comes to know about the patient in the course of his professional work.
  * *(Note: Its disclosure is considered a breach of trust and confidentiality. A patient can sue the doctor for damages if disclosure is made voluntarily without the patient’s consent or valid legal ground)*.

**Examples of Professional Secrecy:**
1. A doctor should not discuss with others about the illness of his patient without consent.
2. A doctor should not disclose a patient's illness to parents or relatives (even though they may pay the fees) if the patient is a major of sound mind.
3. In case of husband and wife, facts of illness of one spouse should not be disclosed to the other without consent.
4. In domestic service or employment, a doctor should not disclose the nature of an employee's illness to the master/employer without the employee’s consent.
5. When reporting a case in a medical journal, care must be taken not to reveal the patient’s identity.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 64

questions.text: Define brain death. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Brain Death:**
* **Brain Death:** Brain death is the irreversible cessation of function of the brain (cortical, brainstem, or both), but in the truest sense cannot be said to be a persistent vegetative state of the person.

**Types of Brain Death:**
1. **Cortical / Cerebral Death (with intact brainstem):** Produces a persistent vegetative state (PVS) where spontaneous respiration continues, but there is total loss of the power of perception and consciousness.
2. **Brainstem Death:** The cerebrum may be structurally intact but functionally disconnected; permanent loss of the vital respiratory center and the ascending reticular activating system (RAS) leaves the patient irreversibly comatose and incapable of spontaneous breathing.
3. **Whole Brain Death / Combined Cerebral and Brainstem Death:** Permanent and irreversible cessation of all functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 142 (also Page 143)

questions.text: What is heat stroke?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Heat Stroke (Heat Hyperpyrexia / Sunstroke):**
* **Heat Stroke / Heat Hyperpyrexia:** Heat stroke is a severe clinical condition resulting from exposure to excessive heat, characterized by a **rectal temperature > 41°C (106°F)** and profound neurological disturbances such as delirium, psychosis, stupor, coma, and convulsions.

**Salient Clinical Features:**
* **Skin:** Characteristically **hot, dry, and flushed with complete absence of sweating** (anhidrosis due to failure of the thermoregulatory sweating mechanism).
* **Pulse & Respiration:** Rapid, bounding pulse which later becomes irregular; rapid, deep breathing (Kussmaul type).
* **Precipitating Factors:** High environmental temperature with high humidity (e.g., 32°C with 100% humidity), heavy exertion, lack of air movement, unsuitable clothing, and dehydration.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 336 & Page 337

questions.text: What are the sentences authorized in Law.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Punishments / Sentences Authorized by Law in Bangladesh (Under Section 53 of the Bangladesh Penal Code - BPC):**
1. **Death sentence (Capital punishment):** Execution by judicial hanging.
2. **Imprisonment for life:** Rigorous imprisonment for life (statutorily computed as 14 years or as defined by the court).
3. **Imprisonment of two descriptions:**
   * a. **Rigorous imprisonment** (with hard labor).
   * b. **Simple imprisonment** (without labor).
4. **Forfeiture of property**.
5. **Fine** (of an amount prescribed by statute or decided at the discretion of the court).
6. **Detention, training, and rehabilitation** (for youthful/juvenile offenders).
*(Note: "Transportation for life" was previously provided, but is now abolished)*.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 22 (Chapter 2: Legal Procedure)

questions.text: What is coup lesion and contra-coup lesion?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Coup and Contre-Coup Brain Lesions:**

* **1. Coup Lesion:**
  * **Definition:** A contusion or laceration of the brain located **directly beneath the site of mechanical impact** on the skull.
  * **Mechanism:** Occurs when the **head is fixed or supported** and is struck by a moving blunt object; the local in-bending of the skull compresses and bruises the cortex directly beneath.

* **2. Contre-Coup (Contrecoup) Lesion:**
  * **Definition:** A contusion or laceration of the brain situated at the **pole diametrically or diagonally opposite to the point of impact**.
  * **Mechanism:** Occurs when the **head is moving / free** and suffers sudden deceleration upon striking a hard, stationary surface (e.g., in falls or RTAs); inertia causes the brain to lag behind, creating cavitation, sudden negative suction pressure, and shear stresses against bony ridges on the opposite side of the skull vault.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 359 & Page 360

questions.text: What are the differences between entry and exit wounds of firearm?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Entry and Exit Wound of Rifled Firearm:**

| Feature | Entry Wound | Exit Wound |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Size** | Usually smaller than the missile (except in contact shots) | Usually larger than the entry wound and missile |
| **Margins** | **Inverted** (turned inwards) | **Everted** (turned outwards) |
| **Shape** | Circular, oval, or cruciate | Irregular, stellate, slit-like, or cruciate |
| **Abrasion & Grease Collars** | **Present** around margins | **Completely absent** |
| **Singeing, Blackening, Tattooing** | **Present** (in close/near range firing) | **Completely absent** |
| **Hemorrhage** | Usually less external bleeding | Profuse and free external hemorrhage |
| **Protrusion of Fat** | Absent | **Fat and torn tissue fragments commonly protrude** |
| **Clothing Fibers** | Carried into the wound tract | Driven outward away from the body |
| **Carbon Monoxide Staining** | Bright red coloration of tissues (in near shots) | Absent |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 280 & Page 281

questions.text: How can you estimate the age of bruise from color change?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Estimation of the Age of a Bruise by Color Changes:**
A bruise resolves through enzymatic degradation of extravasated red blood cells and hemoglobin, following a distinct chronological sequence:

* **Immediately / Fresh:** **Red** (due to fresh, oxygenated hemoglobin).
* **Few hours to 3 days:** **Blue / Dark blue** (due to deoxygenation of hemoglobin).
* **4th day:** **Bluish-black to brown** (due to conversion into **hemosiderin**).
* **5th to 6th day:** **Greenish** (due to breakdown into **hematoidin**).
* **7th to 12th day:** **Yellow** (due to oxidation into **bilirubin**).
* **2 weeks (14 days):** **Completely cleared**; skin returns to its normal color.

*(Note: The color transformation always progresses centripetally—starting at the outer periphery and advancing towards the center)*.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 222 & Page 223

questions.text: When a doctor can refuse to perform medico-legal autopsy?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Conditions in Which an Authorized Medical Officer Can Refuse to Perform an Autopsy:**
1. **Absence of Prerequisite Legal Papers:**
   * a. Absence of the inquest report.
   * b. Absence of the dead body chalan (form 5371).
   * c. Absence of the death certificate / hospital treatment sheet (in cases of hospital death).
2. **Incomplete Prerequisite Papers:**
   * Incomplete or unsigned inquest report or chalan.
3. **Absence of the Escorting Police Constable:**
   * Absence of the police constable authorized to deliver, accompany, and formally identify the dead body.
4. **Death from Highly Infectious Quarantinable Diseases:**
   * Deaths due to catastrophic biological hazards such as plague, anthrax, or viral hemorrhagic fevers (where specialized biosafety mortuaries are unavailable).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 195 & Page 196

questions.text: A baby was brought to emergency department by his mother with the complaint of lacerated injury in right shoulder. In addition to that doctor found multiple injuries of different ages in different part of body? What will be your diagnosis in such a case?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Diagnosis:**
* **Battered Baby Syndrome (BBS)** *(also known as **Caffey’s Syndrome**, **Child Abuse Syndrome**, or **Maltreatment Syndrome**)*.

**Justification for the Diagnosis:**
1. **Injuries in Different Stages of Healing:** Coexistence of fresh trauma (fresh shoulder laceration) alongside older injuries of different ages (e.g., multi-colored bruises, healing abrasions, or old fractures) is the hallmark of repeated, non-accidental trauma.
2. **Multiple Anatomical Sites:** Involvement of multiple, disparate body regions incompatible with a single accidental fall.
3. **Discrepancy in History:** The mother’s single complaint (isolated shoulder trauma) fails to explain the diffuse, widespread multi-age lesions discovered on clinical examination.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 446 & Page 447

questions.text: What do you mean by BMDC? Mention its Functions.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Meaning of BMDC:**
* **BMDC (Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council):** BMDC is a statutory, constitutional, and legal body that regulates medical and dental education and adopts the ethical code of conduct for registered practitioners in Bangladesh.

**Functions of BMDC:**
* **A. Academic Functions:**
  1. Prescribes course curriculum and syllabus for undergraduate medical and dental education.
  2. Maintains standards of undergraduate medical and dental education.
  3. Prescribes standards of postgraduate medical and dental education for the guidance of public universities of Bangladesh.
  4. Prescribes conditions for admission into medical and dental training courses.
* **B. Administrative Functions:**
  1. Grants registration to newly graduated MBBS and BDS doctors.
  2. Maintains and updates the official register of medical and dental practitioners.
  3. Recognizes local medical and dental qualifications.
  4. Recognizes foreign medical and dental qualifications.
  5. Takes disciplinary action (warning notice, temporary suspension, or permanent penal erasure/professional death sentence) for Professional Infamous Conduct (PIC).
  6. Takes legal action against practitioners using false titles or practicing without valid registration.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 51 & Page 52

questions.text: Mention the power of 1st, 2nd and 3rd class Magistrates.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Powers of Judicial Magistrates (Under the Code of Criminal Procedure - CrPC):**

| Class of Magistrate | Imprisonment Term | Solitary Confinement | Maximum Fine | Capital Punishment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **First Class Magistrate** *(includes Metropolitan Magistrate)* | **Up to 5 years** | **Yes** (empowered) | **Up to 10,000 Taka** | Cannot pass death sentence |
| **Second Class Magistrate** | **Up to 3 years** | **No** | **Up to 5,000 Taka** | Cannot pass death sentence |
| **Third Class Magistrate** | **Up to 2 years** | **No** | **Up to 2,000 Taka** | Cannot pass death sentence |

*(Note: They can deal with criminal cases only; only the Sessions Judge Court and High Court Division can pass capital punishment, which must be approved by the High Court Division before execution).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 23 & Page 24

questions.text: Define obscure autopsy.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Obscure Autopsy:**
* **Obscure Autopsy:** Obscure autopsies are defined as autopsies which do not show a definite or clear-cut cause of death, in which there are minimal, indefinite, or subtle post-mortem findings, or where gross lesions are present but their exact significance remains obscure or uncertain.
* *Or,* An autopsy where after gross and microscopic dissection, toxicological analysis, and laboratory investigations, only vague or inconclusive lesions are found that fail to provide an unequivocal anatomical cause of death.
* *(Examples of conditions leading to obscure autopsy: Early myocardial infarction without gross histological change, reflex vagal inhibition, status epilepticus, cardiac channelopathies/arrhythmias, and subtle concealed trauma).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 204 & Page 205

questions.text: Define adipocere formation. Mention its importance.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Adipocere Formation (Saponification):**
* **Adipocere Formation / Saponification:** Adipocere formation or saponification is the formation of a soft, whitish, crumbly, waxy, and greasy material occurring in the fatty or fat-containing tissues of a dead body.
* *Or,* It is a modification of the putrefactive process resulting from the conversion of unsaturated liquid fats into saturated solid fatty acids (palmitic, stearic, and hydroxystearic acids) through bacterial fat-splitting enzymes (primarily *Clostridia*) in a moist, anaerobic environment.

**Medico-Legal Importance of Adipocere Formation:**
1. **Surest sign of death**.
2. **Estimation of time since death:** Provides a rough estimate of the post-mortem interval (commences in 1–3 weeks, takes about 3 months to complete).
3. **Preservation of individual identity:** Facial contours and bodily features remain intact and preserved for years or decades, permitting personal identification.
4. **Preservation of wounds and injuries:** Ante-mortem trauma, cuts, stab wounds, ligature furrows, and firearm marks remain well preserved and recognizable.
5. **Indicates the environment of disposal:** Indicates that the body was immersed in water, buried in moist soil, or kept in a damp, poorly ventilated grave.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 183, Page 184 & Page 185

questions.text: Mention the causes of death due to electrocution.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Causes of Death in Electrocution:**
* a. **Ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest without fibrillation:** Common in arm-to-arm or left arm-to-leg current pathways traversing the heart.
* b. **Paralysis of the respiratory center:** Occurs when the electric current passes through the head or brainstem.
* c. **Respiratory muscle paralysis with secondary asphyxia:** Occurs when low-voltage current produces prolonged tetanic spasms of the intercostal muscles and diaphragm.
* d. **Extensive electrodermal burns and shock:** Caused by high-voltage currents producing massive tissue coagulative necrosis and secondary hypovolemic/burn shock.
* e. **Delayed death:** Occurs hours to days later from severe metabolic acidosis, acute tubular necrosis (myoglobinuria), or secondary wound infection/sepsis.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 349 & Page 350

questions.text: Mention the differences between the ligature mark of hanging and strangulation?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Ligature Mark of Hanging and Strangulation:**

| Feature | Ligature Mark of Hanging | Ligature Mark of Strangulation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Placement / Level** | Placed **high up in the neck** (above the thyroid cartilage, between larynx and chin) | Placed **low down in the neck** (at or below the level of thyroid cartilage) |
| **Direction / Plane** | **Oblique** (slants upwards towards the suspension knot) | **Transverse / horizontal** (encircles neck horizontally) |
| **Continuity** | **Incomplete / non-continuous** (gap present at knot site) | **Complete** (completely encircles the neck continuously) |
| **Base / Floor** | **Pale, hard, dry, yellowish-brown, and parchment-like** | **Soft and reddish** |
| **Abrasions & Ecchymoses** | Rare around the edges of the mark | Common around the edges of the mark |
| **Subcutaneous Tissue** | White, hard, and glistening beneath the mark | Ecchymosed and congested beneath the mark |
| **Damage to Carotid Arteries** | Transverse intimal tears of carotid arteries may be seen | Rare |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 299 & Page 309

questions.text: What are the components of Grievous hurt?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Definition of Grievous Hurt:**
* Grievous hurt is one which is extensive or serious, does not heal rapidly, and leaves a permanent deformity or disfiguration.

**Components of Grievous Hurt:**
*(Must be stated serially as depicted in Section 320 of the Bangladesh Penal Code - BPC)*:
1. **Emasculation** (e.g., excision of penis, castration, or loss of erectile power from spinal trauma).
2. **Permanent privation of the sight of either eye**.
3. **Permanent privation of the hearing of either ear**.
4. **Privation of any member or joint** *(member means an organ or limb performing a distinct bodily function)*.
5. **Destruction or permanent impairing of the power of any member or joint**.
6. **Permanent disfiguration of the head or face**.
7. **Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth**.
8. **Any hurt which endangers life**, or which causes the sufferer to be in **severe bodily pain**, or **unable to follow his ordinary pursuits for a period of 20 days**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 258

questions.text: Mention the character of entry wound of distant shot rifled firearm.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Characteristics of Entry Wound of Distant Shot (>1 meter / >4 meters) Rifled Firearm:**
1. **Size:** Circular or oval hole; usually smaller than or equal to the caliber of the bullet (smaller than when near).
2. **Margins:** Edges are **inverted**.
3. **Shape:** Circular when struck perpendicularly; oval or elliptical when struck at an oblique angle.
4. **Abrasion Collar (Marginal Abrasion):** Narrow, concentric rim of abraded epidermis surrounding the bullet hole due to friction from the spinning bullet.
5. **Grease Collar (Dirt Collar):** Thin, black, greasy ring deposited directly on the margin of the wound defect from barrel oil, lead, and projectile debris.
6. **Burning / Singeing of Hair:** **Completely absent** (flame travels only up to 8–15 cm).
7. **Blackening (Smudging):** **Completely absent** (soot travels only up to 30 cm).
8. **Tattooing (Stippling):** **Completely absent** (unburnt gunpowder flakes travel only up to 60–90 cm).
9. **Carbon Monoxide Staining:** Absent; no cherry-red tissue discoloration.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 274 & Page 275

questions.text: How can you differentiate front seat occupant from driver injuries due to RTAs?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Driver and Front Seat Occupant Injuries in RTAs:**

| Feature | Driver Injuries | Front Seat Passenger (Occupant) Injuries |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Steering-Wheel Impact Injuries** | **Present:** Transverse fracture of sternum, horn-rim imprint, flail chest, cardiac rupture, and transection of the thoracic aorta. | **Completely absent:** Suffers no injuries related to a steering wheel or horn rim. |
| **Impact with Windscreen** | Forehead strikes windscreen producing cuts, abrasions, and superficial lacerations. | Strikes windscreen with greater forward momentum; **more frequently ejected completely out through the windscreen** onto the road. |
| **Impact with Dashboard** | Knees strike dashboard causing patellar fractures and posterior dislocation of the hip. | Knees strike dashboard; **facial and cranial smash injuries** from direct impact against the flat dashboard are more extensive and severe. |
| **Lower Limb Bracing Fractures** | Reflexly braced legs against brake/accelerator pedals sustain compression fractures of the tibia, fibula, or calcaneum. | Bracing against foot-pedals is absent; fractures of the feet or calcaneum are rare unless crushed by floorboard collapse. |
| **Diagonal Seat-Belt Pattern** | Left shoulder-to-right waist diagonal belt mark (in right-hand drive cars). | Right shoulder-to-left waist diagonal belt mark (in right-hand drive cars). |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 368 & Page 370

questions.text: How will you differentiate abdominal pain due to peptic ulcer and starvation?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Abdominal Pain Due to Peptic Ulcer and Starvation:**

| Feature | Abdominal Pain in Peptic Ulcer | Abdominal Pain in Starvation (Hunger Pain) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Cause / Mechanism** | Acid-pepsin irritation and ulceration of gastric or duodenal mucosa. | Intense gastric contractions and hunger spasms occurring in an empty stomach. |
| **Effect of Food Intake** | **Relieved by food/milk or antacids** (in duodenal ulcer); aggravated immediately after food (in gastric ulcer). | **Completely relieved immediately upon ingestion of any food**; recurs only when starvation continues. |
| **Effect of Pressure** | Pressure over the epigastrium **aggravates pain and elicits local tenderness**. | Epigastric pain is **characteristically relieved by firm pressure** (e.g., tying a tight cloth around the abdomen or pressing the epigastrium). |
| **Duration of Pain** | Chronic, periodic, and episodic pain lasting weeks to months. | Pain and hunger pangs are intense during the **first 30 to 48 hours**, after which the sensation of pain subsides into lethargy and weakness. |
| **Associated Symptoms** | Heartburn, dyspeptic acid eructations, water brash, nausea, hematemesis, or melena. | Intense thirst, parched mouth, emaciation, sunken scaphoid abdomen, and subnormal body temperature. |
| **Post-Mortem Findings** | Chronic sharply punched-out mucosal ulcer (often with scarring/fibrosis) at the pylorus or duodenal cap. | Shrunken, contracted stomach with thin, translucent mucosal walls, absent subcutaneous/omental fat, and a distended gall bladder filled with thick, inspissated bile. |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 376 & Page 377

questions.text: Define identification. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Identification:**  
Identification is the determination of individuality of a person based on certain physical characteristics i.e. exact fixation of identity.

**Types of identification:**  
1. **Complete or total identification:** When scientific analysis of different features/data ultimately points a subject as Mr. XX.  
2. **Partial or incomplete identification:** When some features of the person matched with known features of the person searched for but by alone these it may not be possible to point anybody as to be searched for. But these data along with other scientifically approved data available from other sources may ultimately help to establish complete or total identification.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 87 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: Define sexual offence. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Sexual offence:**  
Sexual offence can be defined as sexual intercourse or sex related acts performed in a way which is against the provision of the law of the land.  
*(Or, Sexual offence is the offence where sex related behavior or act which is done against the order of the law of the land.)*

**Classification / Types of sexual offence:**  
1. **Natural offences:** Natural sexual offences are those sexual offences which are performed in the order of nature i.e. by penetration of the female organ (vulva) by the male organ (penis).  
   * *Examples:*  
     * Rape  
     * Incest  
     * Adultery  

2. **Unnatural offences:** These are sexual offences where intercourse is performed against the order of nature i.e. when the act doesn’t involve penetration of a woman’s vagina by the penis of a man.  
   * *Examples:*  
     * Buccal coitus / oral coitus  
     * Sodomy / anal coitus  
     * Tribadism / lesbianism  
     * Bestiality  

3. **Sexual perversion:** Sexual perversions or deviations are persistently indulged sexual acts or fantasies in which complete satisfaction is sought or obtained without sexual intercourse.  
   * *Examples:* Sadism, Masochism, Necrophilia, Fetishism, Transvestism, Exhibitionism, Masturbation, Voyeurism, Frotteurism, Undinism.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 410 *(Concept FM P-3)*

questions.text: Mention the three major systems of blood group with their types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Common / Major blood group systems:**  
1. **ABO system:** Types/Groups are **A, B, AB, and O**.  
2. **Rh factors system:** Types are **Rh +ve (Rh-positive)** and **Rh −ve (Rh-negative)**.  
3. **MN system:** Types are **M, N, and MN**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 529–530 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What do you mean by chelating agent? Give their examples
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Chelating agents:**  
Chelating agents (metal complexing agents) are used in the treatment of poisoning by heavy metals.

**Mechanism of action:**  
These substances act on absorbed metallic poisons. They form chelate with metallic poisons that are freely available in circulation, thus helping their early excretion from the body through the kidney.

**Examples:**  
* **Dimercaprol / British Anti-Lewisite (BAL):** Useful against many metallic poisons e.g. arsenic, copper, mercury, bismuth.  
* **Ethylene-diamine tetra-acetic acid (EDTA):** Best chelating agent for lead.  
* **Desferrioxamine:** Specific antidote for iron.  
* **Penicillamine (cuprimine)**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 559, 560 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What are the signs and symptoms of chronic arsenic poisoning
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Sign-symptoms of chronic arsenic poisoning:**  
* **A. General:** Anemia and weight loss, loss of hair, brittle nail.  
* **B. Skin and nails:**  
  * Finely mottled brown pigmentation, mostly on flexures, temples, eyelids and neck (raindrop type of pigmentation).  
  * There may be rash resembling fading measles rash.  
  * Hyperkeratosis of palms and soles develops in prolonged exposure.  
  * Irregular thickening of nails and Aldrich-Mees’ lines develop in nails of fingers and toes.  
* **C. Ocular:** Congestion, watering of eyes, photophobia.  
* **D. GIT:** Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, salivation.  
* **E. Hepatic:** Hepatomegaly, jaundice, cirrhosis of liver.  
* **F. Respiratory:** Cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea.  
* **G. CVS:** Cardiac failure, dependent edema.  
* **H. Renal:** Chronic nephritis.  
* **I. CNS:** Polyneuritis, anesthesia, paraesthesia, encephalopathy.  
* **J. Hematologic:** Bone marrow suppression, hypoplasia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukemia.

questions.text: Mention the different types of hallucinations with example.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Hallucination:**  
Hallucination is a false sense of perception without any external object or stimulus to produce it. They are purely imaginary, and may affect any or all the special senses.

**Types of hallucination with examples:**  
1. **Visual:** A person imagines being attacked by a lion when no lion exists.  
2. **Auditory:** A person hears voices and imagines a person is speaking to him when no one is present.  
3. **Olfactory:** A person smells pleasant or unpleasant odor when none is present.  
4. **Gustatory:** A person feels good or bad taste, though no food is actually present.  
5. **Tactile/haptic:** A man imagines rats and mice crawling into his bed, when there are none.  
6. **Psychomotor:** A man will have feeling of movement of some body part in absence of such.  
7. **Command:** The patient is ordered by hallucinatory voices to do things/acts.  
8. **Microptic or macroptic:** Any object appears unusually smaller or bigger.  
9. **Sexual:** A person feels sexually satisfied from unfounded self-imaginative objects.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 388 *(Concept FM P-3)*

questions.text: What are the signs and symptoms of chronic lead poisoning
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Sign-Symptom (S/S) of chronic lead poisoning (Plumbism):**  
1. **Facial pallor:** Earliest sign; seen around mouth, due to vasospasm.  
2. **Anemia:** Anemia with punctate basophilia, reticulocytosis, poikilocytosis, anisocytosis, nucleated red cells (sideroblast).  
3. **Burton’s / lead line:** Stippled blue line seen on gum in 50–70% cases (at the junction with teeth, especially in upper jaw due to subepithelial granular deposits of lead sulphide).  
4. **Colic and constipation:** Usually late symptom, seen in 85% of cases.  
5. **Lead palsy / drops:** Late phenomenon, seen in < 10% of cases (wrist drop due to paralysis of extensor muscles of wrist, ankle drop due to paralysis of anterior tibial muscles).  
6. **Lead encephalopathy:** Present in all cases of plumbism and commonly in children.  
7. **Effects on reproductive system:** Sterility in both sexes, menstrual irregularities, abortion.  
8. **Effects on CVS:** Vascular constriction leading to hypertension and arteriolar degeneration.  
9. **Effect on kidneys:** Atherosclerotic nephritis and interstitial nephritis.  
10. **Optic atrophy:** Few patients may develop blindness due to optic atrophy.  
11. **Retinal stippling:** Ophthalmoscopy shows presence of grayish glistening lead particles.  
12. **Lead osteopathy:** Deposition of lead at growing ends may lead to their abnormal development.  
13. **Effects on liver:** Acute or chronic degeneration.  
14. **Effect on peripheral nerves:** Meningoencephalitis and peripheral neuritis.  
15. **Hair:** Alopecia.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 646–647 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: A farmer during his work in the field suddenly experienced of snake bite. What will be your local management?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Local Management / First Aid at the site:**  
1. **Reassurance:** Reassure the victim who may be very anxious.  
2. **Immobilization:** Immobilize the bitten limb with a splint or sling as practiced in fracture of long bone.  
   * If bite is in lower limb, don’t walk.  
   * If bite is in upper limb, don’t move limb.  
3. **Pressure immobilization:** Ideal is to provide pressure immobilization by crepe bandage or long strips of cloth (like Gamcha), wrapped firmly around the entire bitten limb, starting distally around fingers/toes and moving proximally to include a rigid splint. *(Wrapped firmly like for a sprained ankle, but not so tight as to occlude peripheral pulse or prevent a finger slipping between layers; especially helpful for Cobra and Krait bite, not for viper bite).*  
4. **Immediate transfer:** Quickly transfer the victim to the nearest health care facility / hospital while keeping the bitten part immobilized. Avoid allowing anything by mouth.  

**First Aid Methods — NOT RECOMMENDED (What NOT to do locally):**  
* Traditional tight tourniquets.  
* Incisions at the site of snake bite or any other place.  
* Local suction either by mouth or by application of chick.  
* Application of herbal medicines, stones, seeds, saliva, potassium permanganate solution.  
* Ingestion of herbal products like oil, ghee, pepper to induce vomiting.  
* Unnecessary delaying by seeking treatment from 'Ozhas'.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 659–660 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Classify antidotes.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Classification of antidotes:**  
1. **Physical or mechanical antidote:** Prevent action of poison mechanically, without destroying or inactivating damaging actions of poisons.  
   * *Examples:* Demulcents (egg albumin, starch, barley water, milk), Adsorbents (activated animal charcoal), Diluents (water, milk), Bulky food (boiled rice, boiled vegetables).  

2. **Chemical antidote:** Disintegrate and inactivate poisons by undergoing chemical reaction with them.  
   * *Examples:* Weak non-carbonate alkalies for acids, weak vegetable acids for alkalies, common salt for silver nitrate, egg albumin for mercuric chloride, freshly prepared ferric oxide for arsenic, KMnO₄ for opium and other alkaloids.  

3. **Physiological or pharmacological antidote:** Have their own action on different systems of body, producing signs and symptoms opposite to those produced by poisons.  
   * *Examples:* Naloxone for morphine, Neostigmine for Datura or hyoscine group, Barbiturate for strychnine.  

4. **Chelating agents:** Act on absorbed metallic poisons by forming chelate with metallic poisons freely available in circulation, helping early excretion through kidney.  
   * *Examples:* Dimercaprol (BAL), EDTA, Penicillamine (cuprimine), Desferrioxamine.  

5. **Serological antidote:**  
   * *Example:* Anti-snake venom serum (AVS).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 559 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What are the differences between true and feigned insanity?

questions.text: Why ultra-sonogram is better than urinary pregnancy test to detect pregnancy?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Why Ultra-sonogram (USG) is better than Urinary Pregnancy Test (UPT):**  
1. **Direct visualization:** USG visualizes the gestational sac as early as 4–5 weeks and detects fetal pole and fetal cardiac pulsation (cardiac motion can be seen at around 6 weeks), confirming a viable intrauterine pregnancy.  
2. **Identification of location (Ectopic pregnancy):** USG accurately detects ectopic pregnancy, whereas UPT (immunological test for hCG) only detects hCG hormone and cannot differentiate between normal intrauterine and ectopic pregnancy.  
3. **Differentiation from abnormal gestation & pathology:** USG differentiates true pregnancy from molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole), blighted ovum, pseudocyesis, or pelvic tumors/cysts. UPT may show false-positive or abnormally high levels in conditions like hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma.  
4. **Fetal viability and multiplicity:** USG confirms fetal viability (life of fetus) and determines single or multiple gestation (e.g. twins), which cannot be determined by urinary tests.  
5. **Age & EDD estimation:** USG accurately estimates gestational age and expected date of delivery by measuring crown-rump length (CRL), biparietal diameter (BPD), femur length (FL), and abdominal circumference (AC).

**Additional Information (Not Found in Guide Book):**  
*(Note: While the Guide Book extensively covers individual topics including clinical diagnosis of pregnancy, UPT/biological tests on page 467–468, MacDonald's rule/EDD on page 464, and lists USG as an important radiological investigation in pregnancy on page 7, this direct point-to-point comparative reasoning is provided for viva explanation based on standard obstetric and forensic principles.)*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 7 *(Concept FM P-1)*, Page 464, 467–468 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: After snake bite, the victim and a dead snake from the scene of occurrence was brought to the emergency department. How will you identify the snake is poisonous?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Identification of poisonous snake from examination of the dead snake:**  
1. **Belly scales (Ventral scales):** Large and broad, covering the entire breadth of the belly . *(In non-poisonous snakes, belly scales are small and do not cover the entire breadth) .*  
2. **Fangs:** Possesses two long, specialized fangs that are hollow (like hypodermic needles) or grooved . *(Non-poisonous snakes have several small, uniform solid teeth without hollow fangs) .*  
3. **Head scales:** Usually small (as in vipers), but can sometimes be large .  
4. **Tail:** Compressed (e.g. flat/sea snakes) or tapering depending on the species .  
5. **Special identifying features of specific poisonous snakes:**  
   * **Cobra (Elapidae):** Presence of hood with spectacle/monocle mark; 3rd supralabial shield touches the eye and nasal shield .  
   * **Krait (Elapidae):** Subcaudal scales are undivided (single); large hexagonal scales along the middle line of the back (vertebral row) .  
   * **Vipers (Viperidae):** Triangular head covered with small scales; presence of a deep loreal pit between eye and nostril (pit vipers) .

*(Corroboration from victim's bite mark: Poisonous snake bites typically leave two distinct puncture marks / fang marks with or without swelling and oozing, whereas non-poisonous snakes leave a semi-circular row of multiple small uniform teeth impressions) .*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 655, 656 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Define scar. Which scar is used as identification mark?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Scar:**  
Scar is the product of healing of a wound by fibrosis and cicatrization.  
*(Characters: Permanent, made of fibrous tissue, covered by epithelial cells, devoid of hair follicles, pigments and sweat glands, and has less vascularity.)*

**Which scar is used as identification mark:**  
* **True/Permanent scars involving the dermis:** Only injury to the dermis produces a permanent scar (injury to the epidermis does not produce a permanent scar and is only temporary).  
* **Scars with distinct individual peculiarities and permanence:**
  * Surgical scars (e.g. laparotomy, appendectomy, Caesarean section).
  * Vaccination marks/scars (circular or oval, slightly depressed).
  * Burn scars (prominent, irregular, thick, and adherent).
  * Post-traumatic scars indicating weapon type (e.g., linear/straight scar from incised wounds, triangular scar from stab wounds, irregular/thick scar from lacerations).
  * Scars situated at anatomical landmarks (at least two permanent identification marks/scars are noted by the medical officer with their exact site, size, shape, and direction).

questions.text: Mention the signs of chronic lead poisoning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Signs of chronic lead poisoning (Plumbism):**  
1. **Facial pallor:** Earliest sign; seen around mouth, due to vasospasm.  
2. **Anemia:** Anemia with punctate basophilia, reticulocytosis, poikilocytosis, anisocytosis, and nucleated red cells (sideroblast).  
3. **Burton’s line (Lead line):** Stippled blue line seen on the gum at the junction with teeth (especially upper jaw).  
4. **Colic and constipation:** Usually a late symptom, seen in about 85% of cases.  
5. **Lead palsy / drops:** Wrist drop (paralysis of extensor muscles of wrist) and ankle drop.  
6. **Lead encephalopathy:** Headache, insomnia, irritability, hallucinations, and convulsions.  
7. **Effects on reproductive system:** Sterility in both sexes, menstrual irregularities, abortion.  
8. **Effects on CVS:** Vascular constriction leading to hypertension and arteriolar degeneration.  
9. **Effects on kidneys:** Atherosclerotic nephritis and interstitial nephritis.  
10. **Optic atrophy:** May cause blindness.  
11. **Retinal stippling:** Grayish glistening lead particles seen on ophthalmoscopy.  
12. **Lead osteopathy:** Deposition of lead at growing ends of bones.  
13. **Hair:** Alopecia.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 646–647 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: How can you differentiate natural and unnatural sexual offenses?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between natural and unnatural sexual offences:**

| Feature | Natural Sexual Offences | Unnatural Sexual Offences |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition** | Offences performed in the order of nature (by penetration of the female vulva/vagina by the male penis). | Offences performed against the order of nature (where the act does not involve penetration of a woman’s vagina by the penis of a man). |
| **Organs involved** | Male organ (penis) and female organ (vulva/vagina). | Other organs/orifices such as anus, mouth, or involving animals or between same sexes. |
| **Parties involved** | Always between a male and a female. | Between male and male, male and female, female and female, or human and animal. |
| **Examples** | Rape, Incest, Adultery. | Sodomy (anal coitus), Buccal coitus (oral coitus), Lesbianism (tribadism), Bestiality. |
| **Legal Section** | Section 375, 376 (Rape), Section 497 (Adultery) of BPC. | Section 377 of BPC (Unnatural offences). |

questions.text: Mention the contraindication of use of stomach wash tube.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Contraindications of stomach wash / gastric lavage:**

* **A. Absolute contraindications:**  
  * **Corrosive poisoning (except carbolic acid):** Owing to the danger of esophageal or gastric perforation.

* **B. Relative contraindications:**  
  * **Convulsant poisons:** As passing the tube may trigger or precipitate violent convulsions (e.g., strychnine).  
  * **Comatose patients:** Due to the risk of aspiration of stomach contents into the air passages (unless an endotracheal tube with an inflatable cuff is placed).  
  * **Volatile poisons (e.g., kerosene oil):** Which may be inhaled into the lungs causing aspiration chemical pneumonitis.  
  * **Upper alimentary diseases:** e.g., esophageal varices, strictures, or bleeding ulcers.  
  * **Infants and children / Very old subjects.**  
  * **Patient with marked hypothermia or hemorrhagic diathesis.**

*(Mnemonic — **4Cs:** Corrosives [except carbolic acid], Children, Comatose, Convulsions).*

questions.text: How will you take consent for artificial insemination donor?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Consent for Artificial Insemination Donor (AID):**  
1. **Donor's and Donor's Wife's Consent:** Written and informed consent of both the donor and the donor's legally wedded wife is essential.  
2. **Recipient Couple's Consent:** Written informed consent from the recipient woman and her husband must be taken before the procedure.  
3. **Secrecy and Anonymity:** Strict anonymity must be maintained—the identity of the donor should remain secret from the recipient couple, and the donor must not know the identity of the recipient or the outcome of the insemination.

5. **Confidentiality:** Maintenance of strict confidentiality of all records is mandatory.

questions.text: A traveler in deep sleeping condition with rise of body temperature and dilated pupil was brought to you by a passenger and the helper of the bus. What will be your diagnosis and what may be the causes of it?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Diagnosis:**  
**Acute Datura poisoning (Road poison / Traveler’s poison).**

**Causes / Reasons for the diagnosis:**  
1. **Circumstantial Evidence:** The victim is a traveler on a bus. In Bangladesh and India, Datura is commonly termed **"Road poison"** or **"Traveler’s poison"** because criminals administer crushed seeds or extract of Datura mixed with food, drink, tea, or paan to stupefy travelers in order to commit robbery or snatching.  
2. **Clinical Manifestations (Classic Anticholinergic / Morton's Signs):**  
   * **Deep sleeping condition / Stupor:** Datura induces central nervous system depression following delirium, leading to drowsiness, stupor, and coma.  
   * **Rise of body temperature:** Known as **"Hot as a hare"** (hyperpyrexia, temperature can rise up to 105°–107°F due to suppression of sweat gland secretion and central hypothalamic action).  
   * **Dilated pupil:** Known as **"Blind as a bat"** (wide, non-reactive pupillary dilatation causing temporary impairment of accommodation and photophobia due to anticholinergic blockade by hyoscine and atropine).  
   * *Other associated anticholinergic signs:* Dryness of mouth (**"Dry as a bone"**), flushed face/skin (**"Red as a beet"**), and delirium (**"Mad as a wet hen"**).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 601, 602, 604 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Define and classify antidote.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Antidote:**  
Antidotes are substances which prevent action of poison or neutralize poison or produce signs and symptoms opposite to those produced by poison.

**Classification of antidotes:**  
1. **Physical or mechanical antidote:**  
   * *Mechanism of action:* Prevent action of poison mechanically, without destroying or inactivating damaging actions of poisons.  
   * *Examples:*  
     * Demulcents e.g. egg albumin, starch, barley water, or milk.  
     * Adsorbents e.g. activated animal charcoal.  
     * Diluents e.g. water, milk, or similar drinks.  
     * Bulky food e.g. boiled rice or boiled vegetables.  

2. **Chemical antidote:**  
   * *Mechanism of action:* These substances disintegrate and inactivate poisons by undergoing chemical reaction with them.  
   * *Examples:*  
     * Weak non-carbonate alkalies for acids.  
     * Weak vegetable acids for alkalies.  
     * Common salt in case of silver nitrate poisoning.  
     * Egg albumin in mercuric chloride poisoning.  
     * Freshly prepared ferric oxide in arsenic poisoning.  
     * KMnO₄ to inactivate opium and other alkaloids.  

3. **Physiological or pharmacological antidote:**  
   * *Mechanism of action:* These substances have their own action on different systems of body, producing signs and symptoms opposite to signs and symptoms produced by poisons.  
   * *Examples:*  
     * Naloxone — for morphine.  
     * Neostigmine — for Datura or hyoscine group of poison.  
     * Barbiturate — for strychnine.  

4. **Chelating agents:**  
   * *Mechanism of action:* These substances act on absorbed metallic poisons. They form chelate with metallic poisons that are freely available in circulation and help their early excretion from body through kidney.  
   * *Examples:*  
     * Dimercaprol / British Anti-Lewisite (BAL).  
     * Ethylene-diamine tetra-acetic acid (EDTA).  
     * Penicillamine (cuprimine).  
     * Desferrioxamine.  

5. **Serological antidote:**  
   * *Example:* Anti-snake venom serum (AVS) available for snake bite poisoning of both cobra and viper types.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 559 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Define Incest. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Incest:**  
Incest means sexual intercourse by a man with a woman who is closely related to him by blood (prohibited degrees of relationship) e.g. daughter, granddaughter, sister or stepsister, aunt or mother.

**Types / Examples of incest:**  
1. **Between father and daughter** (e.g. Electra complex).  
2. **Between mother and son** (e.g. Oedipus complex).  
3. **Between brother and sister** (e.g. Pharaonic incest).

*(Circumstances where incest occurs: Between mental defectives; where alcohol removes natural inhibitions; in case of cerebral disease e.g. senile cerebral degeneration; when brother and sister have been separated since childhood and meet later as strangers; live in intimacy.)*

questions.text: What are the complications of criminal abortion?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Complications of criminal abortion:**

  * Excoriation, laceration or perforation of vagina, cervix or uterus.

questions.text: Describe the mechanism of action of OPC.

↓

questions.text: How can you differentiate delusion from hallucination?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between delusion and hallucination:**

| Feature | Delusion | Hallucination |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition** | Delusion is a false belief in something which is not a fact, and which persists even after its falsity has been clearly demonstrated. | Hallucination is a false sense of perception without any external object or stimulus to produce it. They are purely imaginary. |
| **Nature of disorder** | Disorder of **thought** (content of thought). | Disorder of **perception** (sensory perception). |
| **External stimulus** | An external object or situation may exist, but the patient forms an erroneous, unshakable belief around it. | Completely absent; perception occurs without any external object or stimulus. |
| **Senses involved** | Not related to special senses; it is an intellectual/mental belief. | Affects any or all of the special senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch). |
| **Types / Varieties** | Delusion of grandeur, persecution, reference, influence, infidelity (Othello syndrome), nihilism, hypochondriacal, self-reproach, erotomania. | Visual, Auditory, Olfactory, Gustatory, Tactile/haptic, Psychomotor, Command, Microptic/macroptic, Sexual. |
| **Common clinical occurrence** | Paranoid schizophrenia, paranoia, dementia, melancholia/depression, delirium tremens. | Organic mental disorders, delirium tremens, schizophrenia, toxic encephalopathies, drug withdrawal, cocaine use. |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 386, 388, 399 *(Concept FM P-3)*

questions.text: How can you say the sample collected from scene of crime containing human blood?
questions.answerMarkdown:
To determine that a sample collected from a scene of crime contains **human blood**, the following step-by-step examination protocol is followed:

1. **Confirmation that the stain is blood:**  
   * **Physical tests:** Naked eye, microscopic examination, and spectroscopic examination.  
   * **Chemical / Screening tests:** Benzidine test (gives blue color), Phenolphthalein/Kastle-Meyer test (deep pink color), Leucomalachite green test, Orthotolidine test.  
   * **Confirmatory microchemical crystal tests:**  
     * *Takayama test:* Pink, feathery crystals of hemochromogen.  
     * *Teichmann test:* Brownish-black rhombic crystals of hemin/hematin chloride.

2. **Determination of human origin (Species differentiation):**  
   * **Precipitin test (Ring test):**  
     * *Principle:* Human blood serum contains proteins in colloidal suspension. When injected into an animal, the animal develops antibodies (antihuman precipitin serum). When human serum comes into contact with this antiserum, precipitins react with human proteins to form a visible precipitate.  
     * *Technique:* A 1:100 saline extract of the bloodstain is placed in a small test tube held in a slanting position, and two drops of antihuman antiserum are added.  
     * *Result:* Formation of a **white ring with well-defined borders at the junction of the two fluids** within 10 to 30 minutes confirms that the blood is of **human origin**.  
   * **Other sero-immunological tests:** Antiglobulin consumption test, mixed antiglobulin test, gel electrophoresis, or ABAcard test.  
   * **DNA Profiling / Typing:** Highly specific confirmation of human origin.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 532, 533 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: On what criteria you will select a donor in case of artificial insemination donor?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Criteria of an ideal donor for artificial insemination by donor (AID):**  
1. **Donor must not be a relative** of either spouse.  
2. **Donor should have had children of his own** (proves proven fertility).  
3. **Donor must be physically and mentally healthy**.  
4. **Donor must be devoid of any hereditary or genetic disease**.  
5. **Racial and physical characteristics** of the donor should resemble as closely as possible to the recipient's husband.  
6. **Donor should be of the same blood group** as recipient’s husband.  
7. **No Rh-incompatibility** between donor and recipient.  

*(Prerequisite / Recommended guidelines:)*  
* Written consent of the donor and his legally wedded wife is essential.  
* Strict anonymity and confidentiality must be maintained (donor must not know recipient's identity, nor recipient know donor's identity).  
* A single donor's semen should not be used to produce more than 10 children.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 458, 459 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Define Impotence & sterility.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Impotence:**  
Impotence is the incapacity or inability of a person to perform the sexual act (intercourse).  
*(Or, Impotence is the physical or psychological inability of either sex to perform normal, complete, and satisfactory sexual intercourse).*

**Sterility:**  
Sterility is the inability of the male to beget children and in the female to conceive children.  

*(Note: Impotence is a ground for divorce and nullity of marriage, but sterility is not).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 450 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Define vitriolage.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Vitriolage:**  
The term vitriolage literally means throwing of oil of vitriol (concentrated sulphuric acid) on the body of a person with the intention to cause bodily injury. But for practical purposes, this term is used in all cases of throwing of any corrosive agent on the body of a person.  

*(Or, Vitriolage can be defined as throwing of any corrosive, mainly concentrated sulphuric acid, on the body, mainly the face of another person, mainly female, for permanent disfiguration with malicious intent or evil motive, mainly by a disgruntled person).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 621 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Mention the types of delusions.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Types / Varieties of Delusion:**  
1. **Delusion of grandeur / megalomania:** The patient believes himself to be a king, god, millionaire, or possessing supernatural powers.  
2. **Delusion of persecution / paranoid delusion:** The patient thinks that people are conspiring against him, trying to harm or poison him.  
3. **Delusion of reference:** The patient thinks that words, actions, or gestures of others or news in TV/newspaper refer particularly to him.  
4. **Delusion of influence / control:** The patient believes his thoughts, feelings, or actions are controlled by some outside power, machine, or radio waves.  
5. **Delusion of infidelity (Othello syndrome):** Morbid and baseless delusion that one’s spouse is unfaithful.  
6. **Delusion of nihilism:** The patient believes that he himself, others, or the whole world does not exist or has ended.  
7. **Hypochondriacal / somatic delusion:** False belief that one is suffering from some terrible, incurable physical disease (e.g. cancer, syphilis).  
8. **Delusion of guilt / self-reproach:** The patient believes he is a sinner, worthless, and responsible for all misfortune.  
9. **Erotomania (De Clerambault’s syndrome):** Delusion that someone, usually of higher social status, is deeply in love with him/her.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 386 *(Concept FM P-3)*

questions.text: Mention the principle of management of poison.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**General principles of treatment and management of acute poisoning:**  
1. **Removal of the patient/victim from the source of exposure:** Especially in cases of volatile or gaseous poisons.  
2. **Removal of unabsorbed poison:**  
   * *Contact poisoning:* Remove clothes and wash affected skin with lukewarm soap-water.  
   * *Ingestion:*  
     * From mouth: Wash mouth.  
     * From stomach: Emesis, stomach wash / gastric lavage.  
     * From intestine: Purgatives or high colonic lavage.  
   * *From site of injection (e.g. snake bite):* Place ligature/splint proximal to site, squeeze or suction.  
   * *Intra-vaginal route:* Vaginal douching with plain water.  
3. **Dilution of poison and delaying its absorption:** By giving water to drink or bulky bland food.  
4. **Elimination of absorbed poison:**  
   * *Diuresis:* Forced alkaline/acid diuresis.  
   * *Diaphoresis:* Using pilocarpine or neostigmine.  
   * *Dialysis:* Hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis.  
   * *Chelating agents* and *hemoperfusion*.  
5. **Use of specific antidotes:**  
   * Physical/mechanical, chemical, physiological/pharmacological, chelating agents, or serological antidotes (AVS).  
6. **Symptomatic and supportive treatment:**  
   * *Safeguard respiration:* Clearing airway, endotracheal intubation, oxygen, artificial respiration.  
   * *Maintenance of circulation:* Treatment of shock, cardiac massage, epinephrine, IV fluids.  
   * *Correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance*.  
   * *Control of convulsions:* Barbiturates, diazepam.  
   * *Control of body temperature:* Management of hyperthermia (cold sponging) or hypothermia (warm coverings).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 554–555 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: How can you say that the lady recently has delivered a child?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Signs-symptoms of recent delivery in a living woman:**  
1. **General appearance (initial 2–3 days):** Exhausted, pale, ill-looking, slight fever, and increased pulse rate.  
2. **Breast changes:**  
   * Breasts are full, enlarged, tender with a knotty feeling.  
   * Nipples enlarged and surrounded by dark areola with prominent Montgomery’s tubercles.  
   * Colostrum or milk can be expressed.  
   * Superficial veins over breasts are prominent.  
3. **Abdominal findings:** Abdominal wall is lax and wrinkled, with striae gravidarum on flanks and linea nigra in the midline.  
4. **Uterine changes (involution):**  
   * On 1st day, the uterus feels like a firm tennis ball with the fundus about 3 cm below the umbilicus.  
   * Decreases in height at about 1.5 cm/day.  
   * By the 6th day, fundal height is midway between umbilicus and pubis.  
   * By the 14th day, fundus reaches the level of the pubic symphysis (becomes a pelvic organ).  
5. **Lochia:** Vaginal discharge having a characteristic sour, disagreeable odor lasting for 2–3 weeks:  
   * *Lochia rubra:* Bright red (1st to 4th–5th day).  
   * *Lochia serosa:* Pale/serous (5th to 8th–9th day).  
   * *Lochia alba:* Yellowish-white or turbid (after 9th day).  
6. **Genital tract findings:**  
   * *Cervix:* Soft and patulous; internal os closes by 24 hours, external os by 2nd week.  
   * *Vagina:* Capacious, relaxed, smooth-walled (loss of rugosity).  
   * *Vulva, Labia, Fourchette:* Swollen, tender, bruised or lacerated; tears of fourchette and posterior commissure.  
7. **Laboratory / Diagnostic findings:**  
   * Pregnancy tests (hCG) remain positive for up to 1–2 weeks after delivery.  
   * USG reveals a bulky, subinvoluted uterus.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 474–475 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: How will you manage a case of snake bite?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Management of a case of snake bite:**  

* **A. First aid at the site:**  
  1. **Reassure the victim:** Allay anxiety and fear.  
  2. **Immobilization:** Immobilize the bitten limb with a splint or sling (do not walk or move the limb).  
  3. **Pressure immobilization:** Apply firm pressure bandage over the bitten limb (especially for Cobra and Krait bites; not recommended for Viper bite).  
  4. **Avoid harmful methods:** Do NOT apply tight arterial tourniquets, do NOT make incisions, suck, or apply chemicals/herbs.  
  5. **Immediate transfer:** Rapidly transport to nearest hospital.  

* **B. Hospital management:**  
  1. **Resuscitation (ABC):** Maintain clear airway, adequate breathing, and circulation.  
  2. **Clinical & laboratory assessment:**  
     * Observe for neurotoxic signs (ptosis, broken neck sign, respiratory paralysis).  
     * Observe for hemotoxic signs (spontaneous bleeding, swelling, blister formation).  
     * **20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT):** Incoagulable blood confirms viperine bite (venom-induced consumption coagulopathy).  
  3. **Anti-Snake Venom (AVS) Therapy:**  
     * *Indications:* Presence of systemic envenomation (neurotoxicity, spontaneous bleeding, incoagulable blood, shock, or local swelling involving more than half of the limb).  
     * *Type:* Polyvalent antivenom (effective against Cobra, Krait, Russell's viper, Saw-scaled viper).  
     * *Dose & Administration:* Initial dose is **10 vials** (diluted in 100 mL normal saline or 5% dextrose water) infused intravenously over 40–60 minutes.  
  4. **Supportive Treatment:**  
     * Tetanus toxoid prophylaxis and broad-spectrum antibiotics.  
     * For neurotoxic respiratory paralysis: Neostigmine with atropine, and mechanical ventilatory support if needed.  
     * For shock and oliguria: IV fluids, treatment of acute kidney injury.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 659–661 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Mention the precautions which need to be taken by the workers who are engaged in spraying insecticides.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Prophylaxis / Precautions for workers engaged in spraying insecticides (OPC):**  
1. Workers should be properly instructed and work should be supervised.  
2. Wear protective clothing of white cotton, a hood to cover head and neck, rubber apron, gloves, and a respirator.  
3. Face and hands should be thoroughly washed with soap and water after spraying.  
4. Not more than **2 hours of spraying in a day** should be done.  
5. Should not work for more than **6 days successively** on spraying.  
6. Should not eat, drink, chew, or smoke in the spraying area.  
7. Spraying machine, tank, container, etc., should be thoroughly washed after use.  
8. Stop spraying immediately if the worker gets a skin rash or feels sick.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 577 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: A skull was recovered from an old grave. From it how can you identify one of the three major races?
questions.answerMarkdown:
The three major races (**Caucasian / Caucasoid**, **Mongolian / Mongoloid**, and **Negro / Negroid**) are identified from examination and metric indices of the skull as follows:

| Feature of Skull | Caucasian (White) | Mongolian (Yellow/Brown) | Negro (Black) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **Cephalic Index (CI)** | **Mesaticephalic** (75–80) | **Brachycephalic** (80–85; short-headed) | **Dolichocephalic** (70–75; long-headed) |
