questions.text: What are the duties and responsibilities of a physician in suspected case of poisoning case management?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Duties of a doctor in case of suspected poisoning:**

1. **Medical duties:**  
   * Care and treatment of the patient gets first priority (immediate resuscitation, removal of unabsorbed poison, administration of specific antidotes, and symptomatic support).

2. **Legal duties / Responsibilities:**  
   * **Note preliminary particulars:** Note name, age, sex, occupation, address, date and time, and at least two identification marks.  
   * **In suspected homicidal poisoning:** Confirm suspicion before expressing an opinion. Once confirmed, request removal of the patient to the hospital.  
   * **Preserve specimens:** Preserve suspected articles of food, drink, vomitus, excreta, and stomach wash samples for chemical analysis.  
   * **Notification to police:**  
     * A *Government Medical Officer* is legally bound to report all cases of suspected poisoning (accidental, suicidal, or homicidal) attended in the hospital to the police.  
     * A *private practitioner* is bound to report to the police or Magistrate if convinced the case is homicidal. (If suicidal or accidental, he is not legally bound to inform the police, but if the patient dies, he must report to the police).  
   * **Dying declaration:** If the condition of the patient is serious, take immediate steps to arrange for the recording of a dying declaration by a Magistrate.  
   * **Death certificate:** If the patient dies, do NOT issue a death certificate; inform the police for post-mortem examination.  
   * **Food poisoning:** Notify the public health authority.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 552 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Why stomach wash is indicated in morphine poisoning though taken IV?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Reason:**  
Stomach wash is indicated in morphine poisoning even after hypodermic or intravenous (IV) injection because **morphine is excreted/re-secreted into the stomach from the circulation through the gastric mucosa**.  

Performing gastric lavage (with a dilute solution of KMnO₄ 1:5000) repeatedly washes out this re-excreted alkaloid from the stomach, preventing its re-absorption into the bloodstream and thereby reducing toxic drug levels in the body.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 583 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: A blood stain was collected from the scene of crime, how can you say it is a stain of female blood?
questions.answerMarkdown:
To determine that a blood stain is of **female blood**, the following sex-specific cellular and genetic criteria are evaluated:

1. **Sex chromatin in White Blood Cells (WBCs):**  
   * Chromosomal pattern is **44 + XX** (in males it is 44 + XY).
2. **Davidson’s body in neutrophils:**  
   * **Present** in female blood. It appears as a small, dense, round/oval nuclear projection shaped like a **"drumstick"** attached to one of the nuclear lobes in neutrophils (seen in about 2–3% or more of female polymorphonuclear leukocytes; absent in males).
3. **Barr body in nucleated cells:**  
   * **Present** in females as a condensed planoconvex mass of heterochromatin lying against the inner surface of the nuclear membrane (derived from the inactive X chromosome; absent in normal males).
4. **DNA Profiling / Sex typing (Amelogenin gene):**  
   * Modern DNA examination shows only the **X-allele (XX)** on amplification of the amelogenin sex-determining gene.

*(Note: If the stain is from menstrual blood, additional features include dark red color, lack of coagulation, acidic reaction, and microscopic presence of desquamated vaginal and endometrial epithelial cells).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 531, 532 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What are the muscarinic effect of organophosphorus poisoning?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Muscarinic manifestations of OPC poisoning:**  
*(Muscarinic effects are more intense than nicotinic effects; OPC increases all secretions):*

1. **Bronchial tree:** Bronchoconstriction (results in wheeze), increased bronchial secretions, dyspnea, cyanosis, and pulmonary edema.  
2. **Gastrointestinal tract (GIT):** Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, tenesmus, and fecal incontinence.  
3. **Cardiovascular system (CVS):** Bradycardia and hypotension.  
4. **Sweat glands:** Increased sweating (diaphoresis).  
5. **Salivary glands:** Increased salivation.  
6. **Lacrimal glands:** Increased lacrimation.  
7. **Pupils:** Marked constriction of pupils (pin-point miosis; occasionally unequal or dilated).  
8. **Ciliary body:** Blurred vision.  
9. **Urinary bladder:** Urinary incontinence.

*(Mnemonic: **SLUDGE** — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Diarrhea, Gastrointestinal distress, Emesis; or **DUMBELS**).*

questions.text: What are the signs of datura poisoning?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Sign-symptoms / Clinical features of Datura poisoning:**  
1. **Dryness of mouth:** Extreme thirst, burning pain in stomach; tongue and mouth dry (dry as a bone).  
2. **Dysphagia:** Difficulty in swallowing.  
3. **Dysarthria:** Difficulty in talking, voice is hoarse and indistinct.  
4. **Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels:** Flushed face and dry, hot skin (red as a beet).  
5. **Diplopia & Photophobia:** Wide, bilateral dilatation of pupils (non-reactive to light) causing temporary blindness (blind as a bat).  
6. **Dry hot skin:** Hyperthermia with temperature rising up to 105°–107°F (hot as a hare).  
7. **Drunken gait:** Staggering, uncoordinated gait due to ataxia.  
8. **Delirium:** Talkative, muttering, restless, picking at bedclothes and imaginary objects (*ludicrous movements*) (mad as a wet hen).  
9. **Drowsiness & Stupor:** Passing into deep sleep or coma.  
10. **Death:** Due to respiratory failure.

*(Summary: **8 D's of Datura poisoning** — Dryness of mouth, Dysphagia, Dilated pupils, Dry hot skin, Drunken gait, Delirium, Drowsiness, Death).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 602 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Mention the management of organo-phosphorus poisoning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Treatment / Management of OPC poisoning:**  

* **A. Decontamination:**  
  1. Remove patient immediately from the source of exposure.  
  2. Remove contaminated clothes.  
  3. Wash exposed skin and body areas thoroughly with soap and water.  
  4. **Gastric lavage:** With 1:5000 KMnO₄ solution if poison was ingested.  
  5. Administer **activated charcoal** in doses of 1 g/kg.  

* **B. Antidote therapy:**  
  1. **Atropine (Pharmacological antidote):**  
     * Start with **2–4 mg IV** (0.05 mg/kg in children) and repeat every 5–10 minutes until **atropinization** is achieved.  
     * *End-points of atropinization:* Clearing of chest secretions (no wheeze/rhonchi), dilated pupils, heart rate > 80 beats/min, dry axillae, and systolic BP > 80 mmHg.  
  2. **Pralidoxime / 2-PAM (Specific cholinesterase reactivator):**  
     * Adult dose: **1–2 g IV** as a 5% solution given slowly over 5 minutes or infused in 150 mL normal saline over 30 minutes. Must be administered before enzyme "ageing" occurs.  

* **C. Supportive care:**  
  1. Maintain a patent airway and suction to remove copious respiratory secretions.  
  2. Oxygen inhalation and ventilatory support (mechanical ventilation) if respiratory failure develops.  
  3. IV Diazepam to control convulsions.  
  4. Antibiotics to prevent secondary pulmonary infection.  
  5. Diuretics to prevent pulmonary edema.  
  6. Strict avoidance of respiratory depressants (Morphine, Aminophylline, Phenothiazine, Reserpine).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 573 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Mention the medico-legal importance of arsenic poisoning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Medico-Legal importance / aspects of Arsenic poisoning:**  
1. **Ideal homicidal poison:** Popularly used as a homicidal agent because it is cheap, easily obtainable, colorless, odorless, tasteless, requires a small lethal dose (0.1–0.2 g), can be mixed undetectably in food/drink, has a gradual onset, and symptoms simulate cholera.  
2. **Disadvantages for homicide (forensic detection):** It retards/delays putrefaction (preserving the body); resists heat; and can be detected in decomposed bodies, charred bones, hair, and nails even years after burial.  
3. **Accidental poisoning:** Common due to contamination of drinking water (sub-soil/tube-well water), use in insecticides, rodenticides, sheep-dips, or medicinal preparations.  
4. **Suicidal poisoning:** Rare because it causes intense, prolonged abdominal pain and agonizing death.  
5. **Abortifacient:** Arsenic preparations are sometimes used locally or internally to procure criminal abortion.  
6. **Cattle poison:** Used maliciously to kill cattle.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 642–643 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Why fingerprint is called 100% data of identification?
questions.answerMarkdown:
Fingerprint system (dactylography) is regarded as **100% data of identification (absolute method without any error)** due to the following reasons:  
1. **Permanence:** Ridge patterns are present from birth on both the epidermis and dermis, remain constant throughout the lifetime of an individual, and cannot be altered except by total destruction of the true skin (dermis).  
2. **Absolute individuality (Uniqueness):** No two fingers or hands in the world have identical ridge patterns, not even in uniovular (identical) twins.  
3. **Mathematical impossibility of duplication:** According to Galton and Quetelet’s calculations, the chance of two individuals having identical fingerprints is estimated to be **1 in 64 billion**.  
4. **Standard of proof:** Comparison and matching of **10 to 12 points of fine characteristics** (minutiae) between prints is universally accepted in courts of law as complete and indisputable proof of identity.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 121, 122 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: How can you say the sample collected from scene of crime containing human blood?
questions.answerMarkdown:
To prove that a sample collected from the scene of crime contains **human blood**, the following standard laboratory procedure is conducted:

1. **Step 1: Confirmation that the stain is Blood:**  
   * **Preliminary / Chemical screening tests:** Benzidine test (produces intense blue color), Phenolphthalein / Kastle-Meyer test (produces deep pink/permanganate color), or Orthotolidine test.  
   * **Microchemical crystal tests (Confirmatory):**  
     * *Takayama test:* Produces pink, feathery crystals of hemochromogen.  
     * *Teichmann’s test:* Produces brownish-black rhombic crystals of hemin (hematin chloride).  
   * *Spectroscopic examination:* Shows characteristic absorption bands of hemoglobin derivatives.

2. **Step 2: Confirmation of Human Origin (Species differentiation):**  
   * **Precipitin test (Ring test):**  
     * *Principle:* Human blood serum contains proteins that act as antigens. When injected into a rabbit, it produces specific antibodies (antihuman precipitin serum).  
     * *Procedure:* A 1:100 saline extract of the bloodstain is placed in a small, narrow test tube, and two drops of antihuman precipitin serum are layered over it.  
     * *Positive finding:* Formation of a **sharp, white precipitate ring with well-defined borders at the junction of the two fluids within 10 to 30 minutes** conclusively proves that the blood is of **human origin**.  
   * **Advanced serological and molecular confirmation:**  
     * Antiglobulin consumption test, gel electrophoresis, or ABAcard test.  
     * **DNA profiling / typing:** Conclusive and infallible confirmation of human origin.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 532, 533 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What are the positive signs of pregnancy?

5. **Ultrasonography (USG):** USG can diagnose pregnancy as early as 6th weeks of conception by visualizing gestational sacs.  
6. **X-ray diagnosis:** Fetal parts can be detected from 16 weeks onwards.

questions.text: What are the differences between true insanity and false insanity?

**Differences between real/true insanity and false/feigned insanity:**

| Feature | Real / True Insanity | Feigned / False Insanity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Onset** | Gradual | Sudden |
| **Motive** | Absent (e.g. no history of commission of crime) | Present (e.g. commission of crime) |
| **Predisposing factors** | Usually present (e.g. history of insanity in parents or sudden monetary loss, grief) | Absent |
| **Signs and symptoms** | Uniform and present whether the patient is being observed or not | Present only when conscious of being observed; variable and always exaggerated and don't resemble any particular mental disease |
| **Facial expression** | Peculiar, e.g. vacant look or fixed look of excitement | No peculiarity; frequently changing, exaggerated and voluntary |
| **Insomnia** | Present | Cannot persist; patient sleeps soundly after a day or two |
| **Exertion** | Patient can stand exertion of fatigue, hunger and sleep for several days without breaking down | Cannot stand exertion for more than a few days and breaks down |
| **Habits** | Dirty and filthy | Not dirty and filthy |
| **Skin and lips** | Dry, harsh | Normal |
| **Frequent examination** | Does not mind | Resents for fear of detection |

questions.text: How can you explain erythroblastosis fetalis?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Erythroblastosis fetalis:**  
In the Guide Book, **erythroblastosis fetalis** is listed as:  
1. An important cause of **stillbirth**.  
2. A recognized natural cause of **infant / neonatal death**.  
3. Under the **Rh blood group system**, an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus is at risk of Rh-isoimmunization.

**Additional Information (Not Found in Guide Book):**  
* **Mechanism:** Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) occurs due to **Rh-incompatibility** between an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive fetus (inherited from an Rh-positive father).  
* During delivery of the first Rh-positive child, fetal Rh-positive red cells enter the maternal circulation, stimulating the mother's immune system to produce anti-Rh antibodies (sensitization/isoimmunization).  
* In subsequent pregnancies with an Rh-positive fetus, maternal IgG anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta into fetal circulation, binding to fetal erythrocytes and causing severe immune hemolysis, severe anemia, jaundice, hydrops fetalis, or intrauterine death/stillbirth.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 503, 509 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: By observing and counting eruption of teeth how can you say the person is of about 14 – 17 years of age?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Estimation of 14 – 17 years of age by observing and counting eruption of teeth:**

1. **Total Number of Erupted Teeth:**  
   * The mouth shows **28 fully erupted permanent teeth** (all incisors, canines, premolars, 1st molars, and 2nd molars are present in both jaws).  
2. **Key Eruption Findings at 12–14 Years:**  
   * **Second permanent molars:** Erupt at **12–14 years**. Their full presence and eruption confirm the person has crossed 12–14 years of age.  
3. **Key Eruption Findings at 17–25 Years:**  
   * **Third permanent molars ("wisdom teeth"):** Erupt at **17–25 years or more**.  
   * In a person aged 14 to 17 years, the third molars have **not yet erupted**.  
4. **Conclusion:**  
   * The presence of the **second permanent molars (total 28 teeth)** and the **absence of eruption of the third permanent molars** establishes the person's age to be **between 14 and 17 years**.

questions.text: What are the factor modifying the effect of poison?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Factors modifying action / effect of poison:**  
1. **Quantity / dose:** More the quantity, more severe will be toxic effects.  
   * *Exception:* CuSO₄ and Alcohol — because they stimulate vomiting in large dose.  
2. **Form of poison:**  
   * *Physical state:* Gases and vapors act more rapidly than liquid. In case of solid, action depends on solubility.  
   * *Chemical combination:* Action depends upon solubility or insolubility resulting from chemical combination.  
   * *Mechanical combination:* Action is altered when combined mechanically with inert substances.  
3. **Concentration / dilution:** Generally, more the concentration more the rapidity of action.  
4. **Mode of administration:** Rapidity of action depends on route of administration.  
5. **Condition of patient / victim:**  
   * *Age:* Poisons have greater effect at two extremes of age.  
   * *State of health:* A healthy person tolerates better than a diseased person.  
   * *Sleep:* Action of poison is delayed if a person goes to sleep soon after taking it.  
   * *Intoxication:* Action is delayed if taken in an intoxicated state.  
   * *Idiosyncrasy:* Some persons are idiosyncratic to certain drugs and react more adversely.  
   * *Habit:* Tolerance develops with repeated use (e.g. drug addicts).  
   * *Cumulative action:* Poisons not excreted readily accumulate in the body when taken repeatedly.  
6. **State of stomach:**  
   * *Food content:* Presence of food in stomach delays action of poison in most cases.  
   * *Empty stomach:* Absorbs poison most rapidly.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 548 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What are the muscarinic effect of organophosphorus compound poisoning?

2. **Gastrointestinal tract (GIT):** Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, tenesmus, and fecal incontinence.  
3. **Cardiovascular system (CVS):** Bradycardia and hypotension.  
4. **Sweat glands:** Increased sweating (diaphoresis).  
5. **Salivary glands:** Increased salivation.  
6. **Lacrimal glands:** Increased lacrimation.  
7. **Pupils:** Marked constriction of pupils (pin-point miosis).  
8. **Ciliary body:** Blurred vision.  
9. **Urinary bladder:** Urinary incontinence.  

*(Mnemonic: **SLUDGE** — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Diarrhea, GI cramps, Emesis; or **DUMBELS**).*

questions.text: What do you mean by XY female?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**XY female (Male pseudo-hermaphroditism / Testicular feminization):**  
XY females are male pseudo-hermaphrodites (also known as *androgyni* i.e. womanly men whose male organs resemble those of female) having a **nuclear sex of XY**, but whose sex organs and secondary sexual characteristics deviate to female form because of testicular feminization.  

* **Causes:** Failure to utilize testosterone due to:  
  1. Androgen receptor deficiency (complete or incomplete androgen insensitivity).  
  2. 5-alpha reductase deficiency (inability to convert testosterone to its active form dihydrotestosterone).  
* **Features / Characteristics:**  
  * Primary amenorrhea.  
  * Female external genitalia.  
  * Short blind-pouch vagina.  
  * Normal size breasts.  
  * Scanty or absent axillary and pubic hair.  
  * Testes are situated in the abdomen or inguinal canal.  
  * Absence of uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries (vas deferens usually present).

questions.text: How will you differentiate pseudo virgin from defloration?

**Differences between pseudo-virgin (false virgin) and defloration:**

| Feature | Pseudo-virgin (False virgin) | Defloration |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hymen** | **Not ruptured** (thick, fleshy, tough, or loose and elastic with folds) | **Ruptured** (shows fresh tear or old healed notches / tags) |
| **Introitus / Vaginal orifice** | May admit 2 fingers, which is not painful | Admits 2 fingers easily without pain |
| **Fourchette** | May show healed tear or remain intact | Ruptured and healed in a thick irregular line |
| **Vagina** | Less rugose and more capacious | Rugosity minimized and more spacious |
| **Fossa navicularis** | More conspicuous | Changed / more conspicuous |
| **Labia minora** | Enlarged, partly pigmented, protrude out through labia majora | Enlarged, partly dark, and projected outside labia majora |
| **Labia majora** | Less fleshy, both sides not in full apposition | Lax and not in close apposition |
| **Breasts** | Variable in size, slightly flabby or moderately pendulous | Enlarge, lose firmness, slightly pendulous |
| **Areola & Nipples** | Areola wider; nipples large and raised | Areola wider; nipples large and raised |

questions.text: A blood like stain was collected from a scene of crime and sent to the Forensic Lab. How will you proceed to examine the stain?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Procedure of examination of a blood-like stain in the Forensic Science Laboratory:**  

1. **Physical and Macroscopic Examination:**  
   * Note the color, shape, size, consistency, and pattern of the stain.  
   * Examine under low-power magnification and ultraviolet (UV) light.  

2. **Chemical Screening Tests (To confirm whether the stain is blood):**  
   * **Benzidine test:** Gives an intense blue color.  
   * **Phenolphthalein test (Kastle-Meyer test):** Gives a deep pink / permanganate color.  
   * **Orthotolidine test:** Gives a green or blue color.  
   * **Leucomalachite green test:** Gives a peacock green / blue-green color.  

3. **Microchemical Crystal Tests (Confirmatory for Blood):**  
   * **Takayama test:** Formation of pink, feathery crystals of hemochromogen.  
   * **Teichmann’s test:** Formation of brownish-black rhombic crystals of hemin (hematin chloride).  
   * **Spectroscopic examination:** Identification of characteristic absorption bands of hemoglobin derivatives (e.g. oxyhemoglobin, methaemoglobin).  

4. **Species Identification (To determine if it is of Human Origin):**  
   * **Precipitin test (Ring test):** Extract of the stain is tested against antihuman precipitin serum; formation of a white ring of precipitate at the junction confirms human blood.  

5. **Individualization & Further Medicolegal Data:**  
   * **Blood grouping:** Determination of ABO, Rh, and MN blood groups.  
   * **Sex determination:** Identifying sex chromatin (Barr body in nucleated cells, Davidson's drumstick body in neutrophils, or amelogenin gene amplification).  
   * **Source:** Differentiating ordinary systemic blood from menstrual blood.  
   * **DNA profiling / fingerprinting:** Unambiguous matching to victim or suspect.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 530–533 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: How will you prevent development of esophageal stricture in case of Sulphuric acid ingestion?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Preventive measures for esophageal stricture following sulphuric acid ingestion:**  
1. **Systemic Corticosteroid Therapy:**  
   * **Prednisolone 60 mg/day** is administered in divided doses early in the course of treatment specifically to prevent esophageal stricture formation and combat shock.  
2. **Immediate Dilution and Demulcents:**  
   * Immediate administration of 250 mL of water, milk, or demulcents (such as egg white, olive oil, melted butter, or liquid paraffin) within half an hour of ingestion to dilute the corrosive acid, reduce tissue necrosis, and soothe the inflamed mucous membrane.  
3. **Rest to the Esophagus (NBM & IV Nutrition):**  
   * Maintain the patient strictly **Nothing by Mouth (NBM)** during the acute destructive phase, providing full parenteral nutrition via the IV route for about one week to allow mucosal healing without mechanical irritation. Gradually transition to liquids and soft diet.  
4. **Mechanical Dilatation (Bougienage):**  
   * Regular prophylactic dilatation using a **mercury-filled bougie of 4 cm diameter** passed daily to maintain esophageal lumen patency and prevent cicatricial contraction and stenosis.  
5. **Broad-spectrum Antibiotics:**  
   * Administer systemic antibiotics to control secondary infection, which prevents excessive scarring and fibrosis.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 617, 620 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Define hymen. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Hymen:**  
Hymen is a fold of mucous membrane about 1 mm thick and usually with an opening, situated at the vaginal outlet partially closing the vaginal orifice.

**Types of Hymen:**  
1. **Semilunar / Crescentic:** Opening is placed anteriorly (most common).  
2. **Annular:** Opening is oval and situated in the center.  
3. **Cribriform:** Perforated by several small openings.  
4. **Septate:** Two lateral openings side by side divided by a central band.  
5. **Vertical:** Opening is vertical.  
6. **Infantile:** Small linear opening in the midline.  
7. **Microperforate:** Tiny opening with a large posterior component.  
8. **Imperforate:** No opening (causes hematocolpos).  
9. **Fimbriated:** Irregular, fringed, or denticulate margins.

questions.text: Define obsession.

**Obsession:**

**Features:**

* Any attempt to resist makes the thought appear more insistent.

* Often associated with dread or fear, compelling the person to indulge in repetitive acts (compulsions) to control anxiety.

questions.text: Mention the importance of 18 years of age.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Medico-Legal Importance of 18 Years of Age:**  
1. **Majority:** Age of attaining legal majority (except when under guardianship of a court of wards, which is 21 years).  
2. **Right to Vote:** Can cast a vote in elections.  
3. **Marriage:** Minimum permissible legal age for marriage for women.  
4. **Kidnapping:** Taking away a girl below 18 years from lawful guardianship without consent constitutes kidnapping.  
5. **Juvenile Offender:** An offender below 18 years is treated as a juvenile offender; above 18 years, the person is tried as an adult.  
6. **Government Service:** Minimum age for entering into government service.  
7. **Factory Employment:** Can engage in any authorized full factory job above this age.  
8. **Testamentary Capacity:** A mentally sound person above this age can execute a legally valid will.  
9. **Valid Consent:** A person above 18 years can give valid legal consent to suffer any harm/surgical procedure resulting from an act not intended or known to cause death or grievous hurt.

questions.text: What are the differences between drug addiction and drug habituation?

**Differences between Drug Addiction and Drug Habituation:**

| Feature | Drug Addiction | Drug Habituation |

| **Dose** | Tendency to increase the dose (tolerance develops) | Little or no tendency to increase the dose |
| **Dependence** | Both psychological and physical dependence present | Some degree of psychic/psychological dependence, but no physical dependence |

questions.text: What will be your legal duties during management of poisoning case?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Legal duties of a doctor in a poisoning case:**  
1. **Primary Duty:** Immediate medical care and resuscitation take absolute priority.  
2. **Identification & Documentation:** Note and record complete particulars of the patient—name, age, sex, address, date, exact time of arrival, and identification marks.  
3. **Preservation of Evidence:** Carefully collect, seal, label, and preserve vomitus, gastric lavage washings, leftover food/drink, urine, and feces for toxicological analysis.  
4. **Notification to Police:**  
   * **Government Medical Officer:** Bound by law to report **all cases** of suspected poisoning (accidental, suicidal, or homicidal) attending the hospital.  
   * **Private Practitioner:** Legally bound to notify the police or magistrate if homicidal poisoning is suspected. (Reporting is not mandatory for purely suicidal/accidental cases while the patient is alive).  
5. **Dying Declaration:** If the patient's condition is serious and deteriorating, make immediate arrangements with a magistrate to record a **dying declaration**.  
6. **In Case of Death:** Never issue a routine death certificate; preserve all specimens, keep the body untouched, and notify the police for an autopsy/inquest.  
7. **Food Poisoning:** Promptly notify the public health authorities if food poisoning is suspected.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 552 *(Concept FM P-4)*, Page 23, 25 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: How will you proceed to examine a hair like substance found in a scene of crime to get information?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Forensic Examination of a Hair-like Substance:**  
1. **Physical & Macroscopic Examination:**  
   * Examine under low-power magnification and oblique lighting to note color, length, curvature, curliness, presence of roots or cut ends, and foreign stains (blood, semen, paint, dyes, or singeing).  
2. **Step 1: Confirm whether it is Hair or Fiber:**  
   * Microscopic examination to look for the **anatomical tri-laminar structure** (cuticle, cortex, and medulla).  
   * **Burn test:** Hair burns slowly with a characteristic odor of burning keratin/horn, swelling into a dark crust.  
3. **Step 2: Differentiate Human from Animal Hair:**  
   * Calculate the **Medullary Index (MI)**:  
     * In **human hair**, MI < 0.3.  
     * In **animal hair**, MI > 0.5.  
   * Examine the cuticle (thin, broad, flat scales in humans vs. large serrated/wavy scales in animals).  
   * Perform a **precipitin test** on the protein extract to confirm human species specificity.  
4. **Step 3: Determine the Site/Region of the Body:**  
   * Scalp, pubic, beard, axillary, or eyebrow hair based on cross-sectional shape, thickness, length, and curliness.  
5. **Step 4: Determine Sex:**  
   * Search for **Barr bodies** in intact hair bulb root sheath cells (present in females, rare in males).  
   * Nuclear DNA analysis (Amelogenin gene) from plucked hair root bulbs.  
6. **Step 5: Determine Manner of Removal (Plucked vs. Shed):**  
   * A bulb that is swollen, irregular, and distorted indicates **forcibly plucked hair**; a shrunken, atrophic, smooth bulb indicates **naturally shed hair**.  
7. **Step 6: Individualization:**  
   * Determine ABO blood group via absorption-elution method and perform STR-DNA profiling to match with the victim or suspect.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 117–119 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: What are the signs of lead poisoning?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Signs of lead poisoning (Plumbism):**  
1. **Facial pallor:** Earliest sign; seen around mouth, due to vasospasm.  
2. **Anemia:** Anemia with punctate basophilia, reticulocytosis, poikilocytosis, anisocytosis, and nucleated red cells (sideroblasts).  
3. **Burton’s line (Lead line):** Stippled blue line seen on the gum at the junction with teeth (especially in the upper jaw) due to subepithelial granular deposition of lead sulphide.  
4. **Colic and constipation:** Usually a late symptom, seen in about 85% of cases.  
5. **Lead palsy / drops:** Wrist drop (due to paralysis of extensor muscles of wrist) and ankle drop (due to paralysis of anterior tibial muscles).  
6. **Lead encephalopathy:** Headache, insomnia, irritability, hallucinations, and convulsions.  
7. **Effects on reproductive system:** Sterility in both sexes, menstrual irregularities, abortion.  
8. **Effects on CVS:** Vascular constriction leading to hypertension and arteriolar degeneration.  
9. **Effects on kidneys:** Atherosclerotic nephritis and interstitial nephritis.  
10. **Optic atrophy:** May cause blindness.  
11. **Retinal stippling:** Grayish glistening lead particles seen on ophthalmoscopy.  
12. **Lead osteopathy:** Deposition of lead at growing ends of bones.  
13. **Hair:** Alopecia.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 646–647 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: Mention the medico-legal importance of artificial insemination donor.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Medico-legal importance / problems of Artificial Insemination Donor (AID):**  
1. **Divorce:** If artificial insemination is done without the husband’s consent, it may form a valid ground for divorce.  
2. **Legitimacy:** The child remains illegitimate in case of a widow or unmarried woman, and also in the case of a married woman if the husband does not formally adopt the child.  
3. **Adultery:** Artificial insemination by donor may raise the question/allegation of adultery *(though legally it does not constitute adultery as physical sexual intercourse did not take place)*.  
4. **Natural birth:** The child will be presumed to be the natural legitimate child if the parents do not disclose the fact of AID.  
5. **Incest:** Risk of accidental incest exists between children born by AID and the biological children of the donor.  
6. **Nullity of marriage:** AID is not a ground for nullity of marriage.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 458, 459 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Classify intersex.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Classification / Types of Intersex:**  

1. **Gonadal agenesis:**  
   * Gonads (testes/ovaries) have never developed and nuclear sexing is negative.  
   * Sex chromosomal pattern is '00'.  
   * No morphological feature of either sex is developed at puberty.  

2. **Gonadal dysgenesis:** External sexual structures are present, but gonads fail to develop at puberty.  
   * **a. Turner syndrome:** Condition of 45 (44+X0) chromosomes where morphology is female, but nuclear sexing is male.  
   * **b. Klinefelter syndrome:** Condition of 47 (44+XXY) chromosomes where anatomical structure is male, but nuclear sexing is female.  

3. **True hermaphroditism:**  
   * Very rare condition of bisexuality where the individual possesses two ovo-testes or one testicle and one ovary with external genitalia of both sexes.  
   * Neither gonad is completely functional.  
   * Sex chromatin may be male or female.  

4. **Pseudo-hermaphroditism:** Gonadal tissue of only one sex is present internally, but the external appearance is of the opposite sex.  
   * **a. Male pseudo-hermaphroditism / Testicular feminization:** Nuclear sex is XY, but sex organs and secondary sexual characteristics deviate to female form due to testicular feminization (5-alpha reductase deficiency). *(Also known as androgyni)*.  
   * **b. Female pseudo-hermaphroditism:** Nuclear sex is XX, but sex organs and secondary sexual characteristics deviate to male form due to congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency is most common). *(Also known as androgyne)*.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 99 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: How can you differentiate poisonous & nonpoisonous snake?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between poisonous snake and non-poisonous snake:**

| Feature | Poisonous snakes | Non-poisonous snakes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Belly scales (Ventral)** | Large and cover the entire breadth of belly | Small, do not cover entire breadth |
| **Fangs** | Two long, specialized fangs; hollow (like hypodermic needles) or grooved | Short and solid; no hollow fangs |
| **Teeth** | Two long fangs, few small teeth | Several small, uniform solid teeth |
| **Head scales** | Usually small (vipers), but sometimes can be large (cobras/kraits) | Usually large |
| **Tail** | Compressed | Not much compressed |
| **Habits** | Usually nocturnal | Not so |
| **Bite marks** | Normally leaves two deep impressions (fang marks), with or without swelling and oozing | Leaves a number of small impressions in a row (more than two teeth markings) |

questions.text: On what findings on a dead body you can say it is a case of lust murder?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Findings indicating a case of Lust Murder:**  
1. **Targeted distribution of wounds:** Localized cutting or stabbing directed specifically to erogenous and sexually symbolic areas, namely the **breasts**, **genitalia**, or **lower abdomen**.  
2. **Extreme mutilation:** Severe mutilation or amputation of sexual organs (e.g. slicing of breasts, cutting of vulva/penis) as an extreme manifestation of sadism.  
3. **Presence of seminal stains:** Semen or spermatozoa detected around the genitalia, inner aspect of the thighs, breasts, or clothes, indicating that erection, ejaculation, or sexual acts accompanied the killing.  
4. **Sexual bite marks:** Presence of human bite marks showing suck-mark petechiae on breasts, neck, or thighs.  
5. **Association with coitus / necrophilia:** Evidence of sexual violation occurring immediately before, during, or after death.

*(Lust murder definition: In extreme cases of sadism, murder serves as a stimulus for the sexual act and becomes the equivalent of coitus, the act being accompanied by erection, ejaculation, and orgasm).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 431 *(Concept FM P-3)*

questions.text: How can you say that the sample found in the scene of crime is of human hair?
questions.answerMarkdown:
To determine that a hair-like sample collected from a scene of crime is **human hair**, it is differentiated from animal hair and other fibers using microscopic, physical, and serological examinations:

| Feature | Human Hair | Animal Hair |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **General appearance** | Thin, fine | Thick, coarse |
| **Cuticular scales** | Short, broad, thin, and irregularly annular | Very large with step-like or wavy projections |
| **Cortex** | Thick, well-striated, and broad (4–10 times the width of medulla) | Thin, rarely more than twice as broad as medulla |
| **Medulla** | Continuous, narrow, fragmented, or even absent | Continuous and much wider |
| **Pigment distribution** | Evenly distributed (concentrated toward the periphery/cuticle) | Mostly concentrated near the medulla (central) |
| **Medullary Index** | **Less than 0.3** (\frac{Diameter of medulla}{Diameter of shaft} < 0.3) | **More than 0.5** (> 0.5) |
| **Precipitin test** | **Specific for human proteins** (forms precipitate ring with anti-human serum) | Specific for animal proteins |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 119 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: Define defloration. Mention its signs.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Defloration:**  
Defloration means loss of virginity i.e. experience of sexual intercourse by a woman for once at least. *(NB: A single sexual intercourse doesn’t alter the genitalia much except rupture of hymen).*

**Signs-symptoms of defloration:**  
* **A. Genital signs:**  
  * **Hymen:** Usually ruptured.  
  * **Fourchette:** Ruptured and healed in a thick irregular line.  
  * **Fossa navicularis:** Changes (more conspicuous).  
  * **Labia minora:** Enlarged, partly dark and projected much outside labia majora.  
  * **Labia majora:** Lax and not in close apposition.  
  * **Vagina:** Rugosity minimized and more spacious.  
  * **Vestibule:** Spacious with appearance of folds.  
  * **Posterior commissure:** No change (or may show healed tear).  
* **B. Extra-genital signs:**  
  * **Breasts:** Enlarge, lose firmness and slightly pendulous.  
  * **Nipples:** Large and raised.  
  * **Areola:** Wider.  
* **C. Signs of pregnancy:** May present.  

*(Note: Only signs of hymen and fourchette arise after first intercourse; all other signs appear after repeated intercourse. Signs of breast directly due to sex-related acts rather than intercourse alone).*

questions.text: Mention the mechanical antidotes with their mechanism of action.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Mechanical (Physical) Antidotes:**  
* **Mechanism of action:** They prevent the action of poison mechanically, without destroying or inactivating the damaging actions of poisons (they coat the mucous membrane, adsorb poison particles, or dilute and physically trap toxins to delay absorption).  

**Types and Examples:**  
1. **Demulcents:**  
   * *Mechanism:* Form a soothing, protective mechanical coating over the gastric mucous membrane, protecting it from irritation and corrosive attack.  
   * *Examples:* Egg albumin (egg white), milk, starch, barley water, mineral oil, milk of magnesia, aluminium hydroxide gel.  
2. **Adsorbents:**  
   * *Mechanism:* Possess extremely fine particles with enormous surface area that mechanically bind, adsorb, and retain poison molecules within their pores, thereby delaying and preventing systemic absorption from the stomach.  
   * *Example:* Activated animal charcoal (activated carbon).  
3. **Diluents:**  
   * *Mechanism:* Mechanically dilute the concentration of poison in the stomach to minimize local contact injury and retard the rate of mucosal absorption.  
   * *Examples:* Water, milk, or similar bland drinks.  
4. **Bulky food:**  
   * *Mechanism:* Envelops sharp mechanical poisons (like powdered glass) or delays absorption of irritants.  
   * *Examples:* Boiled rice, boiled vegetables.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 559, 561, 562 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: How can you differentiate fetal heart sound from uterine soufflé?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Fetal Heart Sound and Uterine Soufflé:**

| Feature | Fetal Heart Sound (FHS) | Uterine Soufflé |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nature of sound** | Sharp, distinct ticking sound resembling the **ticking of a watch placed under a pillow** | Soft, blowing murmur heard on auscultation |
| **Synchronization** | Synchronous with the **fetal heart rate** (rapid, usually 120–160 beats/min) | Synchronous with the **mother’s arterial pulse** (maternal heart rate, 70–80 beats/min) |
| **Origin / Cause** | Produced by cardiac contractions and closure of fetal heart valves | Caused by the rush of maternal blood passing through the dilated, tortuous uterine vessels |
| **Time of appearance** | Becomes audible at **18–20 weeks** of pregnancy | Heard at the **end of 4th month (16 weeks)** onwards |
| **Diagnostic value** | **Positive / conclusive sign** of pregnancy (confirms fetal life) | **Probable sign** of pregnancy (may also occur in large pelvic/uterine tumors like fibroid) |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 467 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: How can you say that the sample found in the scene of crime is of hair?
questions.answerMarkdown:
To prove that a fiber-like substance collected from a scene of crime is **hair** (and not a synthetic, vegetable, or textile fiber), the following structural, microscopic, and chemical criteria are evaluated:

1. **Microscopic Structure (Anatomical Triad):**  
   * A true hair microscopically reveals three characteristic anatomical layers:  
     * **Cuticle:** Outer layer consisting of overlapping, thin cuticular scales.  
     * **Cortex:** Middle cellular layer containing longitudinal fibrils and pigment granules.  
     * **Medulla:** Central core of cells (present in most hairs, continuous or fragmented).  
   * *Fibers (cotton, linen, silk, synthetic nylon, wool) lack this distinct tri-laminar anatomical configuration.*
2. **Hair Bulb / Root and Tip:**  
   * Intact hair typically displays a characteristic **expanded root / hair bulb** at its proximal end and a **tapering or cut tip** at its distal extremity.
3. **Burning Test (Chemical / Physical Behavior):**  
   * Hair (being made of the protein **keratin** and containing sulfur):  
     * Burns slowly with difficulty, swelling into a dark, crisp bead.  
     * Emits a characteristic **pungent odor of burning horn/hair**.  
   * *(Vegetable fibers like cotton burn quickly with a flash, smelling like burning paper; synthetic fibers melt into hard, smooth plastic beads).*
4. **Solubility Test:**  
   * Insoluble in dilute acids; dissolves when heated with concentrated alkaline solutions (e.g. caustic potash, potassium hydroxide), whereas mineral and plant cellulose fibers behave differently.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 119 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: Define impotency and sterility.

questions.text: Define incest. Mention its importance.

questions.text: Mention the civil importance of insanity.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Civil Responsibilities / Medico-legal Importance of Insanity in Civil Matters:**  
1. **Management of Property:** An insane person cannot enter into valid civil contracts or manage his own property.  
2. **Marriage:** Insanity at the time of marriage makes the marriage contract null and void.  
3. **Divorce:** Incurable insanity for a specified period is a valid ground for divorce.  
4. **Testamentary Capacity:** An insane person cannot make a valid will (testament) unless executed during a valid lucid interval.  
5. **Competency as a Witness:** An insane person is not competent to give evidence in a court of law.  
6. **Voting Right:** An insane person is disqualified from exercising the right to vote.  
**Guide Book Page:** Page 395, 396 *(Concept FM P-3)*

questions.text: What are the compositions of snake venom?

Snake venom is basically a complex mixture of toxalbumins, enzymes, and polypeptides:

* **B. Enzymes:** Phospholipase A, Protease, Hyaluronidase, Cholinesterase, Coagulase, Hydrolase, Transaminase, ATPase.

questions.text: Define and classify antidote.
questions.answerMarkdown:
* **Antidote:** Antidotes are substances that prevent the action of a poison, neutralize a poison, or produce signs and symptoms opposite to those produced by a poison.  
* **Classification:**  
  1. **Physical or mechanical antidotes:** Prevent action mechanically without altering the poison (e.g., demulcents like egg albumin, adsorbents like activated charcoal, diluents like water).  
  2. **Chemical antidotes:** Disintegrate and inactivate poisons by direct chemical reactions (e.g., weak non-carbonate alkalies for acids, common salt for silver nitrate, hydrated ferric oxide for arsenic, KMnO₄ for alkaloids).  
  3. **Physiological or pharmacological antidotes:** Produce systemic actions opposite to those of the poison (e.g., Naloxone for morphine, Atropine for OPC, Neostigmine for Datura).  
  4. **Chelating agents:** Form stable, soluble cyclic ring complexes with absorbed heavy metals for rapid urinary excretion (e.g., BAL, CaNa₂EDTA, Penicillamine, Desferrioxamine).  
  5. **Serological antidotes:** Specific antivenom sera (e.g., polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom serum).  
**Guide Book Page:** Page 559 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What do you mean by atropinization?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Atropinization:**  
Atropinization is the therapeutic endpoint achieved during the administration of intravenous atropine in anticholinesterase (OPC / Carbamate) poisoning, indicating that muscarinic acetylcholine receptors have been adequately blocked.  
* **Signs / Criteria of Atropinization:**  
  1. Drying up of bronchial and pulmonary secretions (clearing of rales and rhonchi; dry chest).  
  2. Dilatation of pupils (mydriasis).  
  3. Heart rate > 80–100 beats/min (tachycardia).  
  4. Dryness of the mouth, tongue, skin, and axillae.  
  5. Systolic blood pressure > 80–90 mmHg.  
**Guide Book Page:** Page 573 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What do you mean by illegitimate child?

An illegitimate child is one that is born out of lawful wedlock, or not within a competent time after the dissolution of marriage by divorce or death of the husband, or born within lawful wedlock when procreation by the husband was impossible (e.g., non-access, impotency, or sterility).

questions.text: What will be the external appearance, chromatin body and chromosomal pattern of turner’s syndrome?

* **Chromatin Body:** **Negative** (Sex chromatin / Barr body is absent, resembling a male nuclear pattern: 0%).  
* **External Appearance / Clinical Features:**  
  * Phenotypically **female** with short stature.  
  * **Webbing of the neck** and low posterior hairline.  
  * **Shield-like / broad chest** with widely spaced nipples.  
  * Cubitus valgus (increased carrying angle at elbows).  
  * Primary amenorrhea and infantile external genitalia (gonadal dysgenesis with streak ovaries).  
  * Coarctation of the aorta and cardiovascular anomalies.

questions.text: What are the information you will get from a sample of blood stain?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Information obtained from a bloodstain sample:**  
1. **Confirmation of Blood:** Whether the stain is actually blood (via chemical screening tests like Kastle-Meyer, Benzidine, and crystal tests like Takayama or Teichmann).  
2. **Species Origin:** Whether the blood is of **human or animal origin** (via Precipitin test / Ring test).  
3. **Blood Grouping:** Determination of ABO, Rh, and MN blood groups (via absorption-elution techniques).  
4. **Sex of the Individual:** Detection of sex chromatin (Barr bodies in nucleated cells, Davidson's drumsticks in neutrophils, or amelogenin gene amplification).  
5. **Source of Blood:** Differentiation between systemic blood, menstrual blood (acidic, non-coagulating, containing endometrial cells), or vomited/hemoptysis blood.  
6. **DNA Profile & Individualization:** STR-DNA profiling to establish identity, matching the sample conclusively to a specific suspect or victim.  
7. **Toxicological / Pathological Information:** Presence of drugs, poisons (e.g., carbon monoxide, alcohol), or disease states (sickle cells, infection).  
8. **Age of Stain:** Estimation of time elapsed since deposition based on physical solubility and spectral changes of hemoglobin.  
**Guide Book Page:** Page 530–533 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Define poison.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Poison:**  
Poison is a substance (solid, liquid or gaseous), which if introduced in living body or brought into contact with any part thereof, will produce ill-health or death by its constitutional or local effects or both.

*(Note: The definition of poison is vague and unsatisfactory because: 1. A substance which is harmless in small quantities may act as a poison and cause death when taken in large amount, and 2. Bacterial toxins are not regarded as poisons in the ordinary sense of the term).*

questions.text: Define sodomy. Mention its types.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Sodomy / Anal coitus / Buggery / Greek love:**

*(Who performs the act is the active agent and on whom the act is performed is the passive agent).*

**Types / Varieties of Sodomy:**  
1. **Pederasty:** Sodomy is called pederasty when the passive agent is a child (that passive child is known as a *catamite*).

questions.text: What do you mean by cephalic index?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Cephalic index / index of breadth:**  
Cephalic index or index of breadth is obtained by multiplying the maximum breadth of the skull measured transversely by 100 and dividing the result by the maximum length of the skull measured before backward.

Cephalic index = \frac{Max breadth of skull}{Max length of skull} × 100

**Types of skull based on Cephalic Index (CI):**  
1. **Dolichocephalic (long headed):** CI is 70–75 (Race: Aryans, Aborigines, and Negroes; due to fusion of sagittal suture).  
2. **Mesaticephalic (medium headed):** CI is 75–80 (Race: Europeans, Chinese, and Indians).  
3. **Brachycephalic (short headed):** CI is 80–85 (Race: Mongolians; due to fusion of coronal suture).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 92 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: What is causes of impotency in female?
questions.answerMarkdown:
*(Note: In Forensic Medicine, a female is considered potent at all ages because woman is the passive agent in the sexual act. Impotency in female manifests primarily as local or psychogenic inability to permit penetration/intercourse or frigidity).*

**Causes of female impotency:**  
1. **Local developmental anomalies:**  
   * Congenital absence of vagina.

2. **Local acquired abnormalities:**

3. **Local abnormalities due to diseases:**

4. **Psychogenic causes / Vaginismus:**

   * Fear of pain, apprehension, or severe guilt regarding sexual intercourse.

5. **General & Neurological causes:**

questions.text: What is running amok?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Running amok:**

Running amok is a psychic disturbance resulting from continued use of cannabis, and is characterized by a peculiar homicidal mania.

**Features:**  
* Marked by a period of depression, followed by violent attempts to kill people (impulse to murder).  
* First kills a person against whom he may have real or imaginary enmity and then kills anyone that comes in his way until the person is killed or overpowered.  
* Characterized by hallucinations and delusions of persecution.  
* Irresistible desire to destroy life and property willfully.  
* May commit homicide out of sexual jealousy, but has no recollection afterwards.

questions.text: Mention the management of kerosene oil poisoning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Management of kerosene poisoning:**  

* **A. Asymptomatic cases:**  
  * Admit for observation; discharge after 24 hours if no symptom develops.  

* **B. Symptomatic cases:**  
  * Remove all contaminated clothing and wash the skin with copious amounts of water.  
  * Evaluate and maintain the ventilatory status of the patient.  
  * Administration of O₂ to all patients with respiratory symptoms.  
  * Some patients (with respiratory failure) may require intubation and ventilatory support.  
  * Nutritional support and IV fluids.  
  * Routine use of antibiotics is not recommended.  
  * Other supportive treatment.  
  * Corticosteroids, activated charcoal, cathartics, mineral oil, and olive oil: **NOT BENEFICIAL**.  

*(Important Note: **Gastric lavage is CONTRAINDICATED** because gastric lavage can lead to aspiration chemical pneumonitis).*

**Guide Book Page:** Page 695 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: What are the differences between true and false insanity?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between real/true insanity and false/feigned insanity:**

| Feature | Real / True Insanity | Feigned / False Insanity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Onset** | Gradual | Sudden |
| **Motive** | Absent (e.g. no history of commission of crime) | Present (e.g. commission of crime) |
| **Predisposing factors** | Usually present (e.g. history of insanity in parents or sudden monetary loss, grief) | Absent |
| **Signs and symptoms** | Uniform and present whether the patient is being observed or not | Present only when conscious of being observed; variable and always exaggerated and don't resemble any particular mental disease |
| **Facial expression** | Peculiar, e.g. vacant look or fixed look of excitement | No peculiarity; frequently changing, exaggerated and voluntary |
| **Insomnia** | Present | Cannot persist; patient sleeps soundly after a day or two |
| **Exertion** | Patient can stand exertion of fatigue, hunger and sleep for several days without breaking down | Cannot stand exertion for more than a few days and breaks down |
| **Habits** | Dirty and filthy | Not dirty and filthy |
| **Skin and lips** | Dry, harsh | Normal |
| **Frequent examination** | Does not mind | Resents for fear of detection |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 394 *(Concept FM P-3)*

questions.text: How can you establish the paternity of a newborn baby?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Establishment of Paternity of a child / newborn baby:**  
1. **Accessibility:** Accessibility of the mother with the alleged father during the probable period/time of conception.  
2. **Paternal likeness:** Morphological resemblance/akinness of the child with the father (features, color, complexion, voice).  
3. **Atavism:** Morphological resemblance of the child with its paternal grandparents or great-grandparents instead of the father due to recombination of genes.  
4. **Developmental defects:** Hereditary transmission of unique congenital defects, deformities, or physical anomalies from parents to offspring.  
5. **Blood group test (Serological exclusion):**  
   * A blood group genotype factor absent in the parents cannot be present in the child.  
   * Over **80% exclusion** can be achieved by testing **ABO, Rh, and MN** systems alone.  
   * Adding HLA typing and serum protein systems provides over **98% exclusion**.  
6. **DNA fingerprinting / profiling:** **Confirmative and conclusive proof** of paternity.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 496 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Why first Rh (+) ve child of Rh (-) ve mother usually does not suffer from erythroblastosis fetalis?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Erythroblastosis fetalis in the Guide Book:**  
In the Guide Book, **erythroblastosis fetalis** is listed under:  
* Causes of **stillbirth** (Page 503).  
* Natural causes of **infant / neonatal death** (Page 509).  
* Medicolegal aspects of the **Rh blood group system** in disputed parentage and incompatibility (Page 530).

**Additional Information (Not Found in Guide Book):**  
* **Intact Placental Barrier during Pregnancy:** During the first pregnancy, fetal red blood cells carrying the foreign Rh antigen (D-antigen) remain physically separated from maternal blood by the intact placental barrier, preventing significant maternal sensitization.  
* **Timing of Sensitization:** Significant entry of fetal Rh(+) erythrocytes into the maternal circulation (feto-maternal hemorrhage) typically occurs **only during labor and delivery** when the placenta separates from the uterine wall.  
* **Delayed Antibody Production:** The mother's primary immune response to the foreign D-antigen takes several weeks to months to synthesize maternal anti-Rh antibodies (initially IgM, which cannot cross the placenta). By the time IgG antibodies are produced, the first child has **already been delivered safely**.  
* **Subsequent Risk:** It is in subsequent pregnancies with an Rh(+) fetus that maternal memory B-cells rapidly produce high titers of anti-Rh IgG antibodies, which cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells, causing erythroblastosis fetalis.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 503, 509, 530 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What do you mean by universal antidotes?

Universal antidote is actually a combination of physical and chemical antidotes. It is used when the exact nature of the poison consumed is not known, or in suspected intake of two or more poisons combined, acting against a wide range of poisons.

**Composition of universal antidote:**  
* **Activated charcoal / burned toast:** 2 parts (acts as an adsorbent for many poisons).  
* **Magnesium oxide / milk of magnesia:** 1 part (neutralizes acid poisons).  
* **Tannic acid / strong tea:** 1 part (precipitates most of the alkaloid poisons).

questions.text: Mention the different types of hallucinations.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Hallucination:**  
Hallucination is a false sense of perception without any external object or stimulus to produce it.

**Types of Hallucination:**  
1. **Visual:** A person imagines being attacked by a lion when no lion exists.  
2. **Auditory:** A person hears voices and imagines a person is speaking to him when no one is present.  
3. **Olfactory:** A person smells pleasant or unpleasant odor when none is present.  
4. **Gustatory:** A person feels good or bad taste, though no food is actually present.  
5. **Tactile / haptic:** A man imagines rats and mice crawling into his bed, when there are none.  
6. **Psychomotor:** A man has a feeling of movement of some body part in the absence of such.  
7. **Command:** The patient is ordered by hallucinatory voices to do things/acts.  
8. **Microptic or macroptic:** Any object appears unusually smaller or bigger.  
9. **Sexual:** A person feels sexually satisfied from unfounded self-imaginative objects.

questions.text: Why stomach wash is given in morphine poisoning though poison was taken intravenously?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Reason:**  
Stomach wash is indicated in morphine poisoning even after hypodermic or intravenous (IV) administration because **morphine is actively excreted and re-secreted from the bloodstream into the stomach through the gastric mucosa**.  

Gastric lavage (using a dilute solution of potassium permanganate, KMnO₄ 1:5000) repeatedly oxidizes and washes out this re-secreted alkaloid from the stomach, preventing its re-absorption into the systemic circulation and thereby lowering circulating toxic drug levels.

questions.text: What are the signs and symptoms of datura poisoning?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Sign-symptoms / Clinical features of Datura poisoning:**  
1. **Dryness of mouth:** Extreme thirst, burning pain in stomach; tongue and mouth dry (dry as a bone).  
2. **Dysphagia:** Difficulty in swallowing.  
3. **Dysarthria:** Difficulty in talking, voice is hoarse and indistinct.  
4. **Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels:** Flushed face and dry, hot skin (red as a beet).  
5. **Diplopia & Photophobia:** Wide, bilateral dilatation of pupils (non-reactive to light) causing temporary blindness (blind as a bat).  
6. **Dry hot skin:** Hyperthermia with temperature rising up to 105°–107°F (hot as a hare).  
7. **Drunken gait:** Staggering, uncoordinated gait due to ataxia.  
8. **Delirium:** Talkative, muttering, restless, picking at bedclothes and imaginary objects (*ludicrous movements*) (mad as a wet hen).  
9. **Drowsiness & Stupor:** Passing into deep sleep or coma.  
10. **Death:** Due to respiratory failure.

*(Summary: **8 D's of Datura poisoning** — Dryness of mouth, Dysphagia, Dilated pupils, Dry hot skin, Drunken gait, Delirium, Drowsiness, Death).*

questions.text: If only a fragments of fingerprints are available then how can you identify the person by it?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Identification from fragments of fingerprints:**  
When only fragments of fingerprints are available, identification is established by **Poroscopy**:  
* **Poroscopy:** Study of the microscopic pores of the sweat glands located on the papillary/friction ridges.  
* **Principle:**  
  1. Sweat gland pores vary in size, shape, number per unit length of ridge, and relative distance from each other.  
  2. These characteristics are permanent and unique to each individual throughout life.  
  3. By comparing the size, shape, and spatial arrangement of **sweat pores (poroscopy)**, or the edges of friction ridges (**edgeoscopy**), absolute identity can be determined even when an incomplete or small fragment of a friction ridge print is available.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 122 *(Concept FM P-1)*

questions.text: According to rule of inheritance of MN system blood groups, how can you exclude alleged father?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Inheritance of MN blood group system:**  
The MN system is based on co-dominant M and N antigens:  
* Blood group **M** has genotype **MM**.  
* Blood group **N** has genotype **NN**.  
* Blood group **MN** has genotype **MN**.  

**Rule of Exclusion:**  
An antigen (M or N) cannot appear in the child unless it is present in at least one of the parents. Therefore, an alleged father can be conclusively **excluded** in the following conditions:

1. **When child possesses an antigen absent in both mother and alleged father:**  
   * If the child is **M (MM)** or **MN** and the mother is **N (NN)**, the child must have inherited the **M gene** from the biological father. Any alleged father who is **N (NN)** (possessing no M gene) is **conclusively excluded**.  
   * If the child is **N (NN)** or **MN** and the mother is **M (MM)**, the child must have inherited the **N gene** from the biological father. Any alleged father who is **M (MM)** (possessing no N gene) is **conclusively excluded**.  
2. **When the alleged father cannot pass an obligatory antigen to the child:**  
   * If the alleged father is **M (MM)**, all his biological children **must inherit an M gene** (i.e. child must be M or MN). If the child is **N (NN)**, the alleged father is **conclusively excluded**.  
   * If the alleged father is **N (NN)**, all his biological children **must inherit an N gene** (i.e. child must be N or MN). If the child is **M (MM)**, the alleged father is **conclusively excluded**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 496, 529, 530 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What are the signs of chronic arsenic poison?

questions.text: Describe the management of OPC poisoning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Treatment / Management of OPC poisoning:**  

* **A. Decontamination:**  
  1. Remove patient immediately from source of exposure.  
  2. Remove contaminated clothes and wash exposed skin thoroughly with soap and water.  
  3. **Gastric lavage:** With 1:5000 KMnO₄ solution if poison was ingested.  
  4. Administer activated charcoal (1 g/kg).  

* **B. Antidote Therapy:**  
  1. **Atropine (Pharmacological antidote):**  
     * Start with **2–4 mg IV** (0.05 mg/kg in children) and repeat every 5–10 minutes until **atropinization** is achieved.  
     * *Signs of atropinization:* Clearing of bronchial secretions, dilated pupils, heart rate > 80 beats/min, dry skin/axillae, systolic BP > 80 mmHg.  
  2. **Pralidoxime / 2-PAM (Specific enzyme reactivator):**  
     * Dose: **1–2 g IV** in 100–150 mL normal saline infused over 30 minutes. Reactivates acetylcholinesterase before irreversible enzyme "ageing".  

* **C. Supportive Care:**  
  1. Maintain clear airway, perform suction of secretions, and give oxygen / ventilatory support.  
  2. Control convulsions with IV Diazepam.  
  3. Administer antibiotics to prevent secondary lung infections.  
  4. Avoid morphine, aminophylline, reserpine, and phenothiazines.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 573 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: How can you sure that the free end of stomach wash tube is within stomach after introduction?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Methods to verify the position of the stomach wash tube inside the stomach:**  
1. **Auscultation by Stethoscope:**  
   * The position of the tube in the stomach can be checked by auscultating over the epigastric region with a **stethoscope** while injecting a small volume of air with the bulb or syringe; a characteristic bubbling / gurgling sound confirms placement in the stomach.  
2. **Water Submersion Test:**  
   * Putting the **outer / upper end of the tube under water**:  
     * If continuous bubbling synchronous with respiration is observed, the tube has entered the **trachea / respiratory tract** (must be withdrawn immediately).  
     * If no air bubbles escape (or only an occasional burp of gas), the tube is safely within the **stomach**.  
3. **Aspiration of Gastric Contents:**  
   * Siphoning or gently compressing the bulb yields gastric juice, mucus, or ingested food particles, confirming that the tube is inside the gastric cavity.  
4. **Length of Insertion:**  
   * Checking the distance mark on the tube: approximately **50 cm** in adults and **25 cm** in children from the incisor teeth confirms that the fenestrated tip has reached the stomach.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 557 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: According to rule of inheritance of Rh system blood groups, how can you exclude alleged father?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Genetics of Rh blood group system:**  
* The Rh antigen (D-antigen) is inherited as a dominant gene D.  
* An **Rh +ve** individual has two possible genotypes: **DD (homozygous)** or **Dd (heterozygous)**.  
* An **Rh −ve** individual has the homozygous recessive genotype: **dd**.  

**Rule of Exclusion:**  
An alleged father can be conclusively **excluded** in the following circumstances:  
1. **When an Rh-negative mother has an Rh-positive child:**  
   * An Rh-negative mother is genotype **dd**.  
   * If her child is **Rh +ve (Dd)**, the child must have inherited the dominant **D-gene** from the biological father.  
   * Any alleged father who is **Rh −ve (dd)** has no D-gene to transmit; therefore, an **Rh −ve alleged father is conclusively excluded**.  
2. **When the alleged father is homozygous Rh-positive (DD):**  
   * A homozygous Rh-positive man (DD) must pass a D-gene to all his offspring, meaning all his children must be **Rh +ve**.  
   * If the child born to an Rh-negative mother (dd) is found to be **Rh −ve (dd)**, a homozygous Rh-positive alleged father (DD) is **conclusively excluded**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 496, 529, 530 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Define impulse. Give example.

**Examples / Types of impulse:**

questions.text: What are the stupefying agents?

questions.text: According to rule of inheritance of ABO system blood groups, how can you exclude alleged father?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Genetics of ABO blood group system:**  
The ABO system is governed by three allelic genes: **A, B, and O**. Genes **A and B are co-dominant**, while **O is recessive**.  
* Group A = Genotype **AA** or **AO**  
* Group B = Genotype **BB** or **BO**  
* Group AB = Genotype **AB**  
* Group O = Genotype **OO**  

**Rules of Exclusion of Alleged Father:**  
1. **First Rule (Classical exclusion):**  
   * An agglutinogen/antigen (A or B) **cannot appear in the blood of a child unless it is present in the blood of at least one of the parents**.  
   * If a child has **antigen A** and the mother is **group O**, the child must have received the A gene from the biological father. Any alleged father who is **group O or group B** is **conclusively excluded**.  
   * If a child has **antigen B** and the mother is **group O**, the child must have received the B gene from the biological father. Any alleged father who is **group O or group A** is **conclusively excluded**.  

2. **Second Rule (Mating / Direct parentage exclusion):**  
   * A parent of **group AB** cannot produce a child of **group O** (because an AB parent must pass either an A or a B gene to the offspring). Thus, if the child is **group O**, an alleged father of **group AB is excluded**.  
   * A parent of **group O** cannot produce a child of **group AB** (because an O parent can only contribute an O gene). Thus, if the child is **group AB**, an alleged father of **group O is excluded**.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 496, 529, 530 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: Mention the indications of justifiable abortion.

**Indications of Justifiable / Therapeutic Abortion (Medical Termination of Pregnancy - MTP):**

questions.text: Describe the principle of management of a case of poisoning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**General principles of treatment and management of acute poisoning:**  
1. **Immediate Resuscitation (Airway, Breathing, Circulation - ABC):**  
   * Clear oral airway, suction of secretions, endotracheal intubation if unconscious.  
   * Oxygen administration or assisted mechanical ventilation if breathing fails.  
   * Maintain blood pressure with IV fluids, vasopressors, and treat cardiac arrhythmias.  
2. **Removal of the victim from exposure:**  
   * Evacuate from toxic atmospheres in gaseous/volatile inhalational poisoning (e.g. carbon monoxide).  
3. **Removal of unabsorbed poison (Decontamination):**  
   * *Skin contact:* Strip off contaminated clothing and thoroughly wash skin with soap and running water.  
   * *Ingestion:* Induce emesis (if conscious and non-corrosive) or perform **gastric lavage / stomach wash** within 3–4 hours (using appropriate lavage solutions or water).  
   * *Gastrointestinal adsorption:* Administer **activated charcoal** (1 g/kg) to adsorb toxins.  
   * *Purgation:* Administer saline cathartics (sodium sulfate) or bowel irrigation.  
4. **Use of specific antidotes:**  
   * Administer physical, chemical, physiological/pharmacological antidotes (e.g. Atropine and Pralidoxime for OPC; Naloxone for Morphine), or chelating agents (e.g. BAL, EDTA for heavy metals).  
5. **Elimination of absorbed poison:**  
   * Forced alkaline diuresis (for salicylates, barbiturates) or forced acid diuresis.  
   * Extracorporeal elimination: Hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or charcoal hemoperfusion.  
6. **Symptomatic and supportive treatment:**  
   * Control convulsions with IV Diazepam.  
   * Maintain fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance.  
   * Regulate body temperature (cooling for hyperpyrexia; warming for hypothermia).  
   * Prevent secondary infections with systemic antibiotics.

**Guide Book Page:** Page 554–555 *(Concept FM P-4)*

questions.text: What are the character of homicidal poisons?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Characteristics / Criteria of an Ideal Homicidal Poison:**  
1. **Physical properties:** Colorless, odorless, and tasteless.  
2. **Solubility & administration:** Readily soluble in food, drink, or medicine without producing any obvious physical change, discoloration, or unpleasant taste/smell to avoid suspicion.  
3. **Toxicity:** Highly toxic, requiring only a very small lethal dose to cause death.  
4. **Availability & cost:** Cheap and easily obtainable.  
5. **Symptoms:** Signs and symptoms should simulate or resemble a natural disease (e.g., arsenic simulating cholera).  
6. **Onset of action:** Serious ill-effects and onset should be gradual or delayed sufficiently long to allow the accused to escape suspicion.  
7. **Antidote:** Should have no specific antidote.  
8. **Postmortem findings:** Should produce no characteristic post-mortem tissue lesions.  
9. **Elimination & detection:** Must be rapidly destroyed, metabolized, or made undetectable in the body by chemical analysis or other tests.  

*(Most commonly used homicidal poisons: Arsenic and Aconite).*

questions.text: Describe the Morton’s classification of datura poisoning.
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Morton’s Signs / Classification of Datura Poisoning:**  
Datura alkaloids (hyoscine, hyoscyamine, and atropine) block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, producing the classic anticholinergic clinical features described by Morton's signs:

1. **Dry as a bone:** Extreme dryness of mouth, tongue, pharynx, and skin due to marked suppression and decrease of salivary, bronchial, and sweat secretions.  
2. **Red as a beet:** Marked flushing and redness of the face and neck due to cutaneous vasodilatation.  
3. **Blind as a bat:** Wide, bilateral dilatation of pupils (non-reactive to light) causing cycloplegia, loss of accommodation, diplopia, photophobia, and temporary impairment of vision.  
4. **Hot as a hare:** Marked hyperpyrexia with body temperature rising up to 105°–107°F due to suppression of sweating and central disturbance of heat regulation.  
5. **Mad as a wet hen:** Restless delirium with hallucinations, confusion, and muttering speech, accompanied by characteristic "ludicrous movements" (picking at bedclothes and grasping at imaginary objects).

**Guide Book Page:** Page 602 *(Concept FM P-5)*

questions.text: What are the differences between delusion and hallucination?
questions.answerMarkdown:
**Differences between Delusion and Hallucination:**

| Feature | Delusion | Hallucination |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition** | A false belief in something which is not a fact, and which persists even after its falsity has been clearly demonstrated. | A false sense of perception without any external object or stimulus to produce it (purely imaginary). |
| **Nature of disorder** | Disorder of **thought** (content of thought). | Disorder of **perception** (sensory perception). |
| **External stimulus** | An external object or situation exists, but the patient constructs an erroneous, unshakable belief around it. | **Completely absent**; perception arises without any sensory object or stimulus. |
| **Senses involved** | Not related to special senses; it is an intellectual/mental belief. | Affects any or all of the special senses (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch). |
| **Types / Varieties** | Delusion of grandeur, persecution, reference, influence, infidelity (Othello syndrome), nihilism, somatic/hypochondriacal, guilt, erotomania. | Visual, Auditory, Olfactory, Gustatory, Tactile/haptic, Psychomotor, Command, Microptic/macroptic, Sexual. |
| **Common clinical occurrence** | Paranoid schizophrenia, paranoia, major depressive disorder with psychosis, dementia. | Delirium tremens, toxic encephalopathies, schizophrenia, drug withdrawal, hallucinogen use. |

**Guide Book Page:** Page 386, 388, 399 *(Concept FM P-3)*

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Auscultatory character** | Sharp, distinct ticking sound resembling the **ticking of a watch placed under a pillow** . | Soft, blowing vascular murmur heard over the lower uterus. |
| **Synchronization** | Synchronous with the **fetal heart rate** (rapid, usually 120–160 beats/min). | Synchronous with the **mother’s radial pulse** (maternal heart rate, 70–80 beats/min). |
| **Origin / Cause** | Produced by fetal cardiac contractions and valvular closure. | Caused by the rush of maternal blood through dilated, tortuous uterine vessels. |
| **Time of appearance** | Becomes audible at **18–20 weeks** of pregnancy . | Heard from the **end of 4th month (16 weeks)** onwards. |
